speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Secretary of State.
In yesterday's issue of Le Droit of Ottawa there was an article which outlines the results of an education assistance program set up by the federal government in 1974. According to that report, an Anglo-Quebecker is worth twice as much as a Francophone outside Quebec. The paper goes on to say that for financial year 1976-1977, grants directed to Anglo-Quebeckers amounted to a total of $90 million-$113 per capita. These funds were supposed to be universal and unconditional. But Francophones outside Quebec for that same year received just about $52 million under the condition that their provincial governments agree to set up French schools. This being the case, would the Secretary of State explain such a difference between grants which seem to be a clear case of discrimination?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON AMOUNT OF GRANTS TO ANGLO-QUEBECERS AND FRANCOPHONES OUTSIDE QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a financial assistance program for provinces to support education for minority groups and teaching of the second language. Figures quoted in Le Droit are inaccurate since they confuse two different things, that is assistance to secondary education in the second language and assistance to education for minority groups as if the whole was directed as assistance to education for minority groups. So those figures are inaccurate and the same thing goes for funds granted to provinces other than Quebec to support education in the French language and, in the province of Quebec to support education in the English language.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-JUDGMENT OF SUPREME COURT OF ONTARIO ON RIGHTS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in response to the commitment made by my colleague, the hon. Minister of Justice, that I might make some comments on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. I should like to read the motion the hon. member said he would be prepared to move should a prima facie breach of privilege be found. The proposed motion reads as follows:
That the portions of the judgment of Chief Justice Evans of the Supreme Court of Ontario, given November 9, 1977, which appeared to restrict the rights of members of parliament to full and accurate reporting in the press, be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
Many important points were made in the discussion on this question, but the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton has done the House a service by focusing what in his view is the essence of the question of privilege, namely, what may appear to restrict the rights of members of parliament to full and accurate reporting in the press.
I have read the judgment, and while I agree with the hon. member that concerns which have been raised are valid and ought to be kept to the forefront at all times, I can find nothing that suggests to me even a prima facie case for a breach of privilege. Chief Justice Evans seems to make it clear early in his judgment that no one, in fact, has been charged with any breach of any regulation. Therefore, it is merely an academic exercise to contemplate whether at some time in the future there may or may not be a breach of privilege. A prima facie case of privilege must exist, in reality, in a concrete instance and not in some potential event which may occur in the future. No one has alleged any specific instance in which the privileges of the House, or those of any member of the House, have been abridged or violated.

With regard to the matters then before Chief Justice Evans, he states the following:
The role of the court is not to grant absolution before sinning nor to deal with academic issues.
If the court is unable to absolve before the committing of sin, and has no opportunity to deal with academic issues, certainly it is not for the House of Commons to deal with a matter that has not yet arisen. I should like to quote from page 42 of the judgment, where we find a paragraph that seems to capsulize the cause of concern of some hon. members. It reads as follows:
Following the authorities set out above, I have come to the conclusion that a member of parliament may utilize information proscribed by regulation 76-644 in parliament and may release that information to the media. However, I hold that the privileges of the member cannot be extended to protect the media if they choose to release the information to the public. Nor do I consider that the "real" and "essential" functions of a member include a duty or right to release information to constituents. The cases indicate that the privilege is Finite and I would not be justified in extending the privilege to cover information released to constituents.
Perhaps we ought to consider what this paragraph means in light of our understanding of parliamentary privilege. Every authority-Erskine, May, Beauchesne and Bourinot-points out that privilege, as it applies to individual members, is ancillary to their role as a member of the house and not as individual persons. We, as individuals, have no privileges. We have these privileges because we are members of the House of Commons, and these privileges are ancillary to the roles we hold as members of the House of Commons. In other words, a breach of privilege occurs only when a member is impeded in the performance of his duty, not as a citizen or a politician but as a constituent part of the House. It is not the member who holds the privilege; it is the House. As a functional part of the House, the member enjoys certain rights and immunities. In his judgment, Chief Justice Evans recognizes this explicitly.
Part of the privileges of the House includes the requirement that any published report of its proceedings be faithful, balanced and accurate. In order to assist the media in meeting this standard, parliament long ago enacted sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Senate and House of Commons Act which extend to the media immunities enjoyed by members in the execution of their duties in parliament.
I draw to the attention of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton and to the House that the possible danger of restricting the rights of members of parliament to full and accurate reporting in the media is already safeguarded by sections 7, 8 and 9 of the Senate and House of Commons Act, because these sections extend to the media the immunities which members enjoy in the execution of their duties in parliament.
Personally, I fail to see how-even in the realm of possibility-the transmission of what members say or, as the hon. member puts it, their right to full and accurate reporting in the press, could be abridged in any way in light of the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act, sections 7, 8 and 9. Of course, these immunities which the media enjoy have been supported by the courts and by parliament in the past. Certainly, in the case before us no reporter, no publisher and no
November 24, 1977

broadcaster has been charged with any offence. No member of parliament has been able to say he certainly has been impeded in having himself fully and accurately reported in the press, which is the essence of the hon. member's question of privilege.

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-JUDGMENT OF SUPREME COURT OF ONTARIO ON RIGHTS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-JUDGMENT OF SUPREME COURT OF ONTARIO ON RIGHTS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
While each House of parliament reserves for itself the right to adjudicate questions of privilege, the courts also regard parliamentary privilege as part of the law of the land. I should like to quote from Erskine May's nineteenth edition, page 201, which reads as follows:
On the other hand, the courts regard the privileges of parliament as part of the law of the land, of which they are bound to take judicial notice. They consider it their duty to decide any question of privilege arising directly or indirectly in a case which falls within their jurisdiction, and to decide it according to their own interpretation of the law.
The decisions of the courts are not accepted as binding by the House on matters of privilege, nor the decisions of the House by the courts.
This statement supports the age-old dichotomy that there are, at any given point in time, two doctrines of privilege, one held by the court and the other held by either House. Erskine May goes on to say:
In practice, however, there is a wide field of agreement on the nature and principles of privilege in spite of the apparent deadlock on the question of jurisdiction.
(1)	It seems to be recognized that, for the purpose of adjudicating on questions of privilege, neither House is by itself entitled to claim the supremacy over the ordinary courts of justice which was enjoyed by the undivided high court of parliament.
I believe it is important to establish, if I may enter my own comment within the quotation, that a House undivided or parliament undivided is unable to claim supremacy in the field of privilege, according to Erskine May. I believe that what I am saying is relevant to what I may say later on. Erskine May goes on to say:
The supremacy of parliament, consisting of the sovereign and the two Houses, is a legislative supremacy which has nothing to do with the privilege jurisdiction of either House acting singly.
(2)	It is admitted by both Houses that, since neither House can by itself add to the law, neither House can by its own declaration create a new privilege. This implies that privilege is objective and its extent ascertainable, and reinforces the doctrine that it is known by the courts.
I make the point, and draw upon Erskine May, to establish the fact that there can be a distinction between the privilege as seen by a court and privilege as seen by parliament in what I have described as an age-old dichotomy. But coming to this particular case, 1 argue that it is not the obligation of Mr. Speaker, nor is it the obligation of the House of Commons, to deal with academic or abstract issues-

subsubtopic: MR. WALTER BAKER-JUDGMENT OF SUPREME COURT OF ONTARIO ON RIGHTS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: It is not academic, nor is it abstract.

speechtext: That is my opinion, and I have seen no evidence that any member has been impeded in the performance of his duties. The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-ll, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few observations in this debate. The economic ills which have plagued Canada for a decade and have dissipated the faith of Canadians in their hope for a secure future have been sadly ignored, misunderstood and miscalculated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in presenting his minibudget and the tax proposals presently before the House.

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
At a time when Canada desperately needs a strong and steady hand to guide our monetary and fiscal policies, and when we need a Minister of Finance with imagination and courage to restore confidence in Canada's future and to heal the malignancy destroying our economy, we are presented with a mini-budget and tax proposals that offer nothing but deficit, debt and despair. The Minister of Finance, in defending his position, adopted a well-known excuse, "I had no choice"-a phrase I must remind the House, which is commonly associated with individuals who know they have erred, who attempt to hide the truth and who offer no solutions.
Does no choice mean that workers in Sudbury, Ontario, or Thompson, Manitoba will have to drift aimlessly in a sea of economic uncertainty? Does it mean Ottawa will have to continue to borrow $23 of every $100 it spends? Does it mean the nearly one million unemployed, and in particular the youth of our country, have no hope for the future? Does it mean there is no hope for the declining dollar? Is the inference that we must sit idly by while it continues to deteriorate? Does it mean we are committed to a deficit of better than $8 billion this year, and similar deficits in the future? Does no choice imply the farmers in my area can expect to receive $1.50 a bushel for corn next year, or those on fixed incomes should prepare themselves for a further decrease in their standard of living because the Minister of Finance has conceded he cannot control inflation?
When the Minister of Finance indicated he had no choice, was he in fact stating government policy, namely, the government had erred, the government had attempted to conceal the truth from Canadians and had no solutions? Perhaps the gravity of the situation can best be summarized by quoting from an editorial appearing in the Toronto Star on November 9, 1977, which stated:
Some strong medicine for Canada: Our economy is in grave trouble, one that finance minister Jean Chretien's mini-budget of last month doesn't even begin to
deal with__It's not enough for Chretien to call for confidence and rail that
"the present wave of pessimism seems to have gone too far," as he did in his mini-budget last month. He can't talk the country back to prosperity; words won't create jobs.
The problem for Canada, and the reason the country is in such an economic mess today, is that the country has lacked strong economic leadership in Ottawa for more than a decade. Economic policies have been based on wishful thinking, subordinated to the exigencies of election campaigns or, as in the case of an industrial strategy, simply allowed to flounder in the bowels of the bureaucracy.
Editorials on our economy are not confined within our geographical boundaries. Indeed, an article which appearing in the Wall Street Journal of October 3, 1977, entitled "The Canadian Dollar," stated in part:
Canada isn't doing so well. It's economy has been tangled up by a government effort to apply compulsory wage and price controls for nearly two years. The experiment has been marked by strikes and a flagging growth in production. Foreign direct investment has dried up and inflation which those price and wage controls was supposed to cure, is currently at a higher level than in the United States.
It went on to say:
While the nation's troubles are frequently attributed to the rise of the Quebec separatists, it would be more accurate to say that the rise of the Quebec separatists is closely related to the country's economic mismanagement.
The article created considerable excitement in Canada and uneasiness in Ottawa. However, the United States, the international community-and, unfortunately, many Canadians- have been slow in recognizing what many of us in Canada have known for several years. We have too much debt, too much unemployment, too much government spending, too much inflation, too little productivity, too little investment capital, too much talk, and too little action. When the Wall Street Journal editorialized that "it would be more accurate to say the rise of the Quebec separatists is closely related to the country's economic management," it was expressing a well-established truism, namely, that a weak economy stimulates division.
The breadwinners in Newfoundland, the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario, the prairies, British Columbia and the north are equally concerned about their present and future security, and the program introduced by the Minister of Finance does not create jobs, does not place food on the table and does not pay for the utilities and rent.
On March 16 this year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated "Canadians are living beyond their means." Few in Canada can match the government's experience and record. In all but one of the last ten years, the federal government has run up a deficit on its accounts.
Federal debt obligations have nearly doubled, with a 99.7 per cent increase between 1966 and 1976, rising to a level of $42.2 billion, or approximately $1,800 for every man, woman and child in Canada. Since 1973 alone, federal securities outstanding have grown by 42 per cent. This excessive spending and living beyond our means has had two unfortunate effects. First, the burden of interest payments from this debt has created a large demand upon federal expenditures and, second, a significant proportion of this debt has been "monetized" by the Bank of Canada, thus increasing the supply of money-a major contributor to the cause of inflation.
Although federal debt outstanding has nearly doubled in the last ten years, the cost of servicing that debt has nearly quadrupled over the same period. Between 1966 and 1977 public debt charges have increased from $1.2 billion to $4.7 billion. Based on estimates of spending, public debt charges will total $5.4 billion in 1978, accounting for more than 13 per cent of federal budgetary expenditures. If Canadians are to live within their means, the example must be established by the federal government.
Canada's growing inability to compete with foreign countries and, in particular, our largest export market, the United States, has virtually produced a trade disaster. Our inability to price exports competitively has immediate consequences for our balance of payments. For example, the trade deficit in manufactured goods rose from less than $4 billion to more than $10 billion in the First half of the decade. The more serious consequences are the effects on Canadian living stand-

November 24, 1977

ards, jobs, and political independence. Some of the effects are obvious now, such as reduced surplus of merchandise trade, a weak and unstable dollar. Other effects that are just becoming apparent are unwillingness of Canadian exporters to expand production capacity and the movement of whole plants from Canada to the United States.
In recent years, Canada has been progressively shifting from a goods-producing economy to a society dominated by services. Although it would be incorrect to indicate all services do not create wealth, we cannot ignore the inescapable fact that innumerable programs depend on the tax dollars of the productive segment of society, or perhaps it would be more accurate to say those sectors which produce real wealth. Less than 3'/2 million of the 10 million Canadians who have jobs are employed in Canada's goods-producing sectors. Two million are employed in the manufacturing sector which is a smaller proportion of the work force than any of our major trading partners. There are 650,000 in construction, and about 800,000 in the primary resources industries. Canada's service sector now employs more than 6'/2 million Canadians. Of this number, approximately 2'h million work in government services, which is a higher proportion of the work force in government services than in Great Britain.
Let me emphasize that the growth in the service sector is a trend among industrialized countries which is accepted by the vast majority of people. I have no doubt those present in this chamber are sympathetic to programs which, for example, assist our senior citizens or those less fortunate individuals who are unable to provide for their own needs. The central issue, and the question that must be asked, is whether Canada can afford the innumerable services that are offered or contemplated. The evidence is quite clear-that Canada has and is attempting to support a higher level of services with a lower level of goods-producing activity than any of the major industrialized countries.
Not infrequently Sweden is used as the yardstick for comparative purposes when one is discussing social and economic problems, and one cannot escape the harsh reality that Sweden has a larger manufacturing sector and a smaller service sector than Canada. The effects of this imbalance are obvious. Canada has become less competitive. This imbalance has affected productivity, it has impaired our ability to provide capital for the creation of jobs in the private sector and, as I indicated earlier, it has affected our balance of trade, resulting in the largest trade deficit in our history. It has affected the confidence of Canadians with respect to future economic growth, as well as impairing our ability to control inflation.
Canada's emphasis on services of all kinds has meant not only that services have been absorbing a disproportionate share of investment capital that could be used more efficiently for productivity improvements, but the smaller, hard-pressed goods-producing sectors are not creating the wealth upon which present services can be maintained or upon which an expanded services sector must be based. The existing stagna-
Income Tax
tion in the Canadian economy has prompted certain groups and individuals, depending on their perception or bias, to emphasize a particular symptom.
Excessive wage rates, decreased productivity, too many services, excessive government spending, corporate rip-offs, lack of business initiative, and a host of other factors have been espoused as the causes creating the present situation. However, it is apparent that Canada can no longer price its goods competitively for the international market and, in particular, for the United States. The anti-inflation program has not restored a competitive position. The federal government, by following an economic policy which can best be described as "good economics are bad politics, and good politics make poor economics", has no other strategy. Obviously, inflation must be brought under control, at least to a rate which is in line with our major competitors.
Mr. Speaker, if Canada is ever to become more than an exporter of raw resources, the manufacturers and processors must be able to price their goods to meet the requirements of our major trading partners. On February 20 of this year, Milton Friedman stated: "There is only one place inflation is made in Canada, and that's in Ottawa."
Who is he?
Although Mr. Friedman's remarks refer to his beliefs about the relationship-
Who is he?

I will answer the hon. member's question when I have finished. Although Mr. Friedman's remarks refer to his beliefs about the relationship between money and inflation, the statement is also appropriate for describing the lack of concern shown by the whole government sector over cost inflation within its own expenditures. When one indicates that a particular group within the economy is bearing the burden of inflation-the suggestion refers to a group which is either unwilling or unable to raise its own income to compensate for price increases of goods and services-then sir, if income does not grow as rapidly as prices, the amount purchased must decrease and in times of rapid and continuous price increases those living on fixed incomes bear the greatest burden of inflation. For example, someone who retired in 1970 with a fixed pension of, say, $6,000 would find in 1976 that that amount of money would purchase a 1970 equivalent of $3,917 in goods and services. If the $6,000, had been the sole source of income, that person's standard of living would have dropped by 35 per cent.
Many Canadians have suffered as a result of inflation and, at times, price increases have been resisted by consumers. For instance, a reduction in coffee consumption, the weak housing market in many cities, and the reduced sales of automobiles in 1975 all indicate that Canadians can be resistant to burdensome price increases. Superficially, government resembles Canadians in that they, too, are faced with higher costs. However, unlike Canadians, there is much less incentive for government to resist price increases, and its income is always

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
growing more rapidly. There is even less incentive for government, as the prospect of the need to borrow is not seen to deter spending. During the period between the third quarter of 1970 and the third quarter of 1976, government spending increased by 148 per cent. Although several reasons are advanced for increased government spending, one obvious explanation is the propensity for a public service to proliferate, once established, and the difficulty to terminate such a service.
One example may serve as an illustration. During examination of the estimates of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, we calculated that between $50 million to $75 million had been mismanaged by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in its handling of one program, namely, the Indian economic development fund. No one questioned the merits of the program and the necessity to develop an economic base in the Indian community which would promote greater self-sufficiency and less dependence on welfare programs. However, sir, the government's insistence to embark on grandiose projects has left in its wake many multi-million dollar projects which have gone bankrupt and the public perception that the Indian community has failed.
At least one reserve, the Millbrook band in Nova Scotia, has called for a public inquiry into the Abenaki Inn to clear their name. I have asked the Auditor General, under the new powers of the auditor general's act, to investigate the entire program and report his findings to the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, this program is not an isolated finding, and I am convinced that if the various departments were forced to question and examine more carefully existing and future programs, millions of dollars would be saved or would be utilized far more effectively.
In the time remaining, I would like to briefly touch on two specfic issues. First of all, it will not surprise the minister or the government to learn that I have received considerable correspondence relating to the federal government's proposed changes for the taxation of life insurance. I have no doubt the minister's decision to withdraw the budget proposal which would have taxed a portion of life insurance proceeds payable at death was the direct result of the combined concern and effort of millions of policyholders across Canada. I know many of my constituents shared concern and voiced their objections to that particular part of the bill.
I was initially tempted to congratulate the minister for his announcement during the speech from the throne. However, at the risk of sounding ungrateful, I hesitated to do so for two reasons. First, I am persuaded to conclude that the minister's announcement was one of political expediency and he has yet to convince me, or the vast majority of policyholders in Canada, that the basic policy of this government, namely, the confiscation of the rights of a life insurance policyholder, has been altered.
There can be no doubt that the federal government, in deciding to tax policyholders to satisfy their insatiable needs and their appetite for additional monies, knew perfectly well they were confiscating the long-established rights of the individual policyholders. I would ask: Would the minister have

withdrawn the budget proposal which would have taxed a portion of life insurance proceeds payable at death if public concern had not been voiced? I suggest the answer would have been "no". I ask again, sir, have the minister and the government altered their basic policy regarding the rights of the individual policyholder? Again, the answer is "no".
I would say to the minister, in all sincerity, that until such time as he rescinds the proposal to tax the policyholder at the time of taking out a policy loan, as well as rescinding his proposal to disallow the deduction of policy loan interest as an expense, he is infringing upon the rights of policyholders. As I indicated previously, the basic issue is that of the rights of individual policyholders who number approximately 12 million throughout Canada. If the minister recognizes those rights, his course of action is clear and the proposals will be rescinded. If the minister does not recognize this fundamental right and insists on retaining the proposals in the legislation, then he must be accountable, not only to my party but to the 12 million policyholders in Canada.
Finally, I wish to make a brief comment on the proposed $100 million for job creation. Even the most optimistic proponents of the plan recognize this will have a minuscule effect on the nation's unemployment rate, which is expected to top 10 per cent this winter.
It is not my intention to take issue with present government job-creation policy at this time which, on balance, has led to an ever-increasing demand for government supported social services and has done little to create permanent jobs. Rather I want briefly to refer to changes that should be promoted by Canada Manpower which would contribute immeasurably to increasing job opportunities.
During October of this year, James G. O'Neill, Jeannette Jackson, Cindy Merritt and Cheryl Stonefish, presented their findings on the status of skilled trades in Kent county, Ontario. The document was an in-depth study of skilled trades in Kent county, and despite a present unemployment rate which is fairly high they found there is an immediate need for over 300 skilled tradesmen and a projected need of approximately 2,700 for present and future vacancies. The implications of this are profound. Although a number of groups were mentioned as contributing to the problem, Canada Manpower was singled out. I quote from page 95 of that document, where it is stated:
The majority of respondents believe that Canada Manpower is a bureaucratic institution which is not in tune with small business and industry. Its effectiveness as a recruitment centre is diminishing and the agency is not promoting its programs or fulfilling its expectations. The numbers of young people looking for positions are not directed into apprenticeship programs which are available. Rather, it is the responsibility of the applicant to find his own position and then enrol in an apprenticeship. If Canada Manpower is to provide its anticipated function, it must become more responsive to the needs of its applicants and it must be aware of apprenticeship openings and make this information available. The services of Canada Manpower is supposed to be counselling and perhaps this aspect should be stressed. Too often an applicant must search out his own jobs and many applicants are unaware of available apprenticeships.
The point I wish to make is that the government should be giving top priority to imaginative, constructive studies such as
November 24, 1977

proposed by the authors I have mentioned, and sponsored, incidentally, by Mr. Ronald F. Moon, president of Local 127, UAW. I have no doubt that a commitment to such a project would produce permanent jobs for a far more appreciable portion of the labour force in my area.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks today will concern the whole topic of employment and unemployment, but first I should like to review three main points of a thesis I put forward in the debate on the speech from the throne which relate to unemployment but are more general in nature. I should like to place them in the context of the theme we are discussing today.
The points I made were these: There has been a quantum jump in the problems which governments throughout the world have been called upon to face in recent years. The inflation figure, at 1.5 per cent in the OECD countries over the last 100 years, has now risen to basically 5 per cent. Unemployment generally has become more acute. I referred to Sweden, where the rate would run at about 6 per cent if it were recorded in the same way as ours. Similar unemployment rates are faced by Japan and a number of other countries.
The second point I made was that economic and fiscal techniques usually employed Keynesian theories, and so on- are proving unsuccessful. Third, there is the new notion of shortages, particularly of energy shortages. I concluded we were probably at the end of an era dominated by the idea of growth, and that new ideas must be introduced. I did not say then, and I do not say now, that growth will not be a major concern in the economic sphere. But it will not be the only one. We shall have to take a fresh look at all the things we are doing. It is within this context, I believe that we must look at the whole issue of employment and unemployment.
A couple of weeks ago, on November 9 or 10, we are given the employment and unemployment figures for this country taken as of the week ending October 15. We saw, of course, that the adjusted rate of unemployment was 8.3 per cent and that the unadjusted rate was 7.3 per cent. One of the things we did not hear very much about was the fact that as of the end of that week there were 257,000 more Canadians working than had been working in the same week a year earlier. Little was said about the fact that in the month of August 10,260,000 Canadians were working-the largest work force in the history of this country.
A great deal of gloom has been cast on this whole employment question. Recognition is not being given to the fact that we are creating jobs in this country faster than in any of the OECD countries. The rate of job creation between October, 1976, and October, 1977, was 2.3 per cent, representing a significant achievement. The problem remains, of course, that in the same month 780,000 Canadians were shown as unemployed. Some would argue that the real figure is higher. It may be higher, or it may be lower, depending on how the question is phrased.
Two techniques have traditionally been used to deal with unemployment. The first is to offer increased incentives to
Income Tax
business in an effort to encourage the creation of new jobs. This has been the method favoured by fairly right-wing Conservatives in the past. I do not label any of the parties in this House as such, because there are such wide swings in all our parties. Another method which is used-and it follows Keynesian theories closely-is to put more money into circulation by lowering income tax, or by other fiscal and monetary means, as a way of increasing demand. This has been, perhaps, the more progressive way of doing things and it is one which has worked, more or less, since the depression of the thirties.
In the budget introduced in the spring of this year, the government employed both methods. It laid out about $1.2 billion on incentives to business, and it laid out some money- not a very large amount-on the demand side. But in addition to the money laid out in the budget on the demand side, there was the income tax indexing provision which also has the effect of stimulating demand. In addition, there was the increase in old age pensions, and so on, bringing the total put into the demand side, as of January 1, to an amount in the neighbourhood of $2.2 billion. I am also including the effect of such programs as Canada Works. That sum is very close to the amount which the New Democratic Party feels should be spent on the demand side.
In the mini-budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) produced a month ago, there was provision of a further $800 million or $900 million, and if we consider the indexing which will occur as of January 1, 1978, we arrive at a figure of $1.5 billion. So, in slightly over 12 months a sum of between $4 billion and $4.5 billion has been put into the demand side. I do not know how anyone can sit on the opposite side and say we have not tried to do something on the demand side. Do not forget that this is in addition to $1.2 billion which we put on the business incentives side, yet we have unemployment figures of 8.3 per cent adjusted and 7.3 per cent unadjusted. These figures will likely get worse through the winter months.
Mind you, there are very strong reasons why we have such high unemployment. In addition, the economy has some sluggish qualities in it. One is the fact that this year we will have something in the order of 300,000 more people coming into the work force, which is about five times the number coming into the work force in the fifties. The work force is growing at a much faster rate than any other country, and this presents us with some problems.
I should like to look at the demand techniques because I am concerned about them. As I say, we will probably put something in the order of $4 billion to $4'/2 billion into demand techniques by January 2, 1978. However, I would like to indicate that I do not think these techniques are working, and I do not think the solutions proposed by the opposition, particularly by the NDP, will be effective in any really significant way. I do not think that an extra $214 billion, as suggested by the NDP will create anything in the order of 300,000 jobs. I

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
just do not think this is a possibility, and I disagree with it entirely.
One reason I think it will not work is that the level of saving in this country has become very significant. We have had an unusual situation occurring over the last five years, where Canada leads the "Big Seven"-the summit group of members of the OECD countries, the United States, Great Britain, France, West Germany, Japan, Italy and Canada-with the largest increase in personal consumption expenditure of any of these nations namely, 6.5 per cent on average. At the same time, we have had the second largest increase in the household savings ration; the savings ratio has increased in only one other country, a very strange phenomenon.
The OECD group says the reason for this phenomenon is that we have created so many more jobs in this particular period, and therefore there is more income around to be distributed. I am concerned with the savings ratio itself, and I should like to give the House the definition of "personal savings" because I think it is important in terms of creating demand. According to Statistics Canada, personal savings are considered to be the residual amount after deducting personal expenditures on consumer goods and services and after deducting direct personal tax payments and other current transfers from total income.
It is interesting to note that in 1970 personal savings represented 5.3 per cent of personal disposable income in Canada. By 1976 that had grown to 9.5 per cent, close to double. As a matter of fact, in 1975 it did double-savings in 1976 were a little less. This presents a very serious problem when one seeks to use the demand method for increasing economic activity and creating jobs. The problem is that if you reduce personal income tax or other taxes, such as sales tax, one might be creating additional savings which, again, would be removed from the demand side, and we would not get the kind of results we expect.
There are other techniques which might be used to create employment. Certainly, direct work employment projects are being used by the government and there might very well be more of these projects. But I am not sure whether we can expect very much from these other areas. I hear a great deal particularly from all three opposition parties about industrial strategies, and I know there is a great deal of concern in the government about the whole notion of industrial strategy. But I do have some worry about this particular notion, especially since I see what is happening to Sweden, a country which has done a great deal in terms of industrial strategy. Sweden is one of those countries which has put its eggs into a few baskets, one of them being high quality steel and the bottom has more or less dropped out of the steel market. Thus, Sweden finds itself in great difficulty. I am not so sure at this particular point that the industrial strategy notion is going to be as effective as perhaps we hoped it might be. I do not say that we should not be considering it or that we should not look at other techniques alongside a new industrial strategy; but I do say that we should look at it with a great deal of care.

I should like to talk about what I think will be one of the concerns for the future in terms of employment, given the fact that we will have continuing growth in the work force and that this country and most other countries are experiencing the same kind of problem. I think there will be much more interest in the future in the notion of work-sharing. What do I mean, Mr. Speaker, by work-sharing? I mean the simple technique of trying to adjust the number of jobs which are available, the useful work that needs to be done in this country, to the number of people available to do it. There seems to be a degree of equity in this kind of notion, in the sense that one group is not expected to do all the work, while the other group is never plugged-in to the job market but shares some of the benefits. In this way we have a degree of equity, and I think this is something we should look at very carefully.
I had an experience which I should like to relate to hon. members of the House in connection with work-sharing which I think illustrates the problem we are facing. As a former high school principal of a fairly medium-sized school of 1,200 students and 70 or 80 teachers during the early 1970's I had an experience which I think is worth relating. During the 1960s and up to about 1970 there was massive growth in the school systems of this country as a result of the great influx of young people coming into the schools. There was a great deal of upward mobility on the part of teachers because new schools were being opened. There were jobs for principals, vice-principals, department heads, and so on, and this led to a great dependence on upward mobility as a means of getting ahead, as a means of creating incentives.
Then all of a sudden, Mr. Speaker, within the space of about one year, all of this growth stopped. The number of young people coming into the schools was reduced considerably and the demand for teachers fell right off. We were left with a very frustrating situation, a situation of no growth which few other parts of society were experiencing-and, as I say, a great many frustrations flowed from this. I think one of the causes of a lot of stress in the academic field to the dissatisfaction of teachers in the last four or five years, certainly in high schools and elementary schools, stems from this lack of growth, this lack of upward mobility on the part of teachers. I lived through a year or so of this, and I was very concerned about the possible effect in this particular scene. Therefore, we looked at several ways in which we might ameliorate this situation. There are many techniques that could be used, and we tried a couple. There were some which we advocated but we were not very successful in the achieved results.
One technique involved early retirement. It seemed a reasonable proposition that at a certain point those who wanted to retire early should be allowed to do so, and some incentive could be added to encourage this kind of thing. The second technique was phased retirement, and in terms of the school system phased retirement refers to a person perhaps teaching half a day or assuming half a teaching load for three periods instead of six periods a day. There would be some kind of pairing with another person doing the same kind of thing.

The third technique had to do with pairing itself. In this case, you might possibly have two people on the staff who only wanted to work part-time. It might involve a married woman who wanted to be at home more and in this way she was able to pair with some other person doing the same kind of thing. It is very interesting to note that where this pairing has been done-and there are some statistics on this-the school, or wherever it was done, benefited considerably in that it received more than 50 per cent of the work from each of the individuals forming the pair. Therefore, this worked very successfully.
Another form of work-sharing is, of course, straight leave of absence. Another form, and one that interested me a great deal, was the notion of sabbatical leave. A teacher could go on a sabbatical leave. His salary would be reduced. If he was at the top of his salary range and his salary was reduced to two-thirds, it would be very easy to hire a new teacher at the bottom level of the salary range to replace him for the remainder of that year. These were some of the techniques we looked at in respect of schools.
When I first came to parliament these ideas were fresh in my mind. While we have had no discussions about work-sharing until the last month or two, I have always been concerned and interested in the possibilities of using these techniques. Having done a little research on the subject, I find there is a great deal being done in terms of work-sharing in Europe at the present time, particularly in West Germany as well as in countries such as Japan. Instead of laying people off in a given industry because of economic fluctuations, attempts are made to share the work with employees working a six-hour day, or whatever is involved in the amount of sharing required. I found, also, that there is a considerable amount of work-sharing in parts of the United States, particularly in California. In all these areas there has been a considerable amount of success. One of the points I mentioned earlier is that people working shorter days are not less productive, but probably are more productive. You have work-sharing in the form of pairing with increased productivity on the part of the two people involved.
I am very interested in the efforts the federal government is making at the present time in this connection, particularly in the project at Bathurst, New Brunswick, involving the notion of work-sharing using the unemployment insurance fund. This is something well worth looking at. When considering the scene at Sudbury and the lay-offs at INCO and Falconbridge, I can fully understand the views of the labour movement rejecting, at least in the beginning, the whole notion of worksharing, because it is in their own interests and in the interests of the community that the number of people involved in work-sharing be reduced considerably. It is possible to create other kinds of jobs and move people to other places like Elliot Lake or to the Syncrude project. This should be done in the first instance, of course.
However, at some point I believe there will be people laid off at Sudbury. I hope these lay-offs do not occur in carte blanche fashion or just in respect of new employees but, rather, that there is an element of work-sharing. If the situation is handled
Income Tax
this way, it would be a good step forward. We could use the unemployment insurance fund to compensate a whole group of employees whose work is reduced, rather than having some employees laid off completely and drawing unemployment insurance.
One of the advantages of work-sharing is that there is leisure time available. A miner who works only four days a week would have much more leisure time. This probably would be of great value to many people. In terms of the INCO situation, I would like to see the government at some later point, not right now, make an inquiry among those employees and, for that matter, employees all across the country, to determine how many would voluntarily choose some form of work sharing with a reduced work week or a reduced hourly day. I am sure we would find, as a result of a canvass that many people would accept this on a voluntary basis, thus creating many job openings in the country. I am sure that many people working five days a week or 40 hours a week would voluntarily accept a shorter work week or a shorter work day. In this way, we would have a number of jobs filled by other people.
This is a slight divergence, but I must say I am disturbed at the statements about the INCO situation in relation to EDC funds being used to create sales of mining equipment to update mines in other parts of the world. This is of my concern because I am sure that in my community of Thunder Bay the same attitude would not obtain. In the last two or three years, to my knowledge, we have had two very sizeable orders placed with Canada Car, both funded by EDC: one was for Poland and involved tree farmers for the woods industry in that country, and one involved Mexico and the purchase of rail cars. Each of these orders could in some way eventually create competition for Canadian industries, I suppose, but we will also find that as these countries become more industrialized, they will be in a position to purchase more of the sophisticated technology we are to produce. I think it is a great mistake to criticize this kind of thing. Somebody else would have done it, of course, but these particular orders which amounted to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100 million have had a significant effect on our community.
The government should seriously consider this whole notion of work-sharing. It should undertake a study to determine how many people across the country would voluntarily accept this concept. Work-sharing should not be introduced on a compulsory basis, even at places like Sudbury where lay-offs are a fact, but should always be voluntary. The government would then know how many people would be willing to forgo some work time and some wages, because we are speaking basically in terms of the same hourly wage, but shorter hours or a shorter week, in favour of more leisure time in which to do the other things they would like.
There are many employees in various industries in this country, some of whom are blue-collar workers, who have a fair degree of savings. Perhaps some of these workers would

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
welcome this leisure time in order to do something else with that time. Many people have things going on the side. Many people have small farms, and so on: they would welcome the same kind of leisure time. Many Canadians are working 40 hours a week, punching the clock, and so on, in our industries. Some of them are very valuable people to their communities. We should adopt the idea which I refer to as the guaranteed annual role. That would enable people, who have something to contribute to their communities, to find the time to do so. These are some of the things which can happen if we had a voluntary survey.
There seems to be a concern, because we are sharing the work, that we are not doing anything to increase demand. I am not sure that is true. If a person was on a four-day voluntary week, his savings would be somewhat less, and therefore probably he would spend a higher portion of his income than otherwise. Actually, that may generate more demand even though we are not creating more jobs.
In terms of work-sharing and the people who may look at it favourably, there is another area I should like to deal with. A Swedish economist and social scientist developed a thesis in a texbook known as "The Harried Leisure Class". The thesis was that those who are fairly affluent, earning $20,000 or more a year, are working more hours than those who are not so affluent, and their leisure time is reduced by their work time. I suppose most hon. members would fit into that category. Because of this affluence, they have a fair amount of money to spend. Therefore, their consumption time is fairly long: they spend a great deal of time in stores buying things, having things fixed, and so on. As people become more affluent and more busy, they have less leisure time. Leisure time is the time when people are not sleeping, consuming or working. When Canadians see themselves in a fairly affluent state, spending a great deal of time buying goods they may not need, they may look at leisure time as something which is much more valuable. Most hon. members would see leisure time as something which is valuable. This is another area where volunteers may be found for reduced days and reduced hours.
In conclusion, Canadians would do very well to look partially at one solution for some of our economic and unemployment problems, that is, work sharing. By that, I mean matching up the number of jobs available in this country with the number of people available for them. I am referring to useful jobs. Creating unuseful jobs does not work to the betterment of Canadians. If these things are looked at, I am sure one of the techniques of the future will most certainly be work sharing.

Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to take part in this debate even in its dying moments. One might say that because Bill C-ll reveals the major weaknesses of the government's economic policies. My constituents, as well as others, are entitled to know what I think about these matters. Basically, this is a bill which gives incentives to private industry in the hope that it will provide jobs. It has failed in this effort. To me and to many hundred thousand Canadians the present rate of unemployment is by far the most serious weakness in our economy. Improving the
[Mr. McRae.)
unemployment picture should be the first priority in all our policies.
It is one thing to quote statistics, which I propose to do, but it is quite another to grasp the actual meaning in the lives of people of large-scale unemployment. There is a serious danger that we will become insensitive to the facts underlying national statistics and will be unwilling to adopt an economic strategy which will end the mismanagement of the economy and make a serious impact on the matter of unemployment.
The most recently issued statistics indicate that the rate of unemployment across Canada is approximately 8 per cent. If adequate attention is paid to those unemployed but not on the lists, it is estimated the amount would be approximately 10 per cent, or over a million Canadians. This is the worst rate of unemployment since 1940, but it fails to indicate that in various parts of the country-and I am thinking of the Atlantic provinces in particular-there are serious depression levels of unemployment being inflicted on workers.
Behind these statistics is a picture of individual human suffering and pain. The hopes and lives of families, older workers and women workers, are shattered by unemployment. Of the unemployed, 421,000 were men and 414,000 were women. Of the total, 418,000 were workers under 25, and 128,000 were workers between 45 and 64. I hate to think what is happening to the younger people under 25 when nearly half a million of them are unemployed. The average duration of unemployment is said to be 14.5 weeks. There were 667,000 families hit by unemployment. Many of the Canadians who experienced unemployment were family men.
The myth frequently repeated about unemployment is that a lot of it is voluntary. The facts of life and the statistics show the contrary. During the second quarter of this year there were only 43,200 full-time vacant jobs in Canada, according to Statistics Canada. Therefore, for every 100 persons unemployed there were only five vacant jobs. This means if every job had been filled, 870,800 workers would still be out of work, or 77.6 per cent of the work force would still be jobless.
Another myth which is frequently accepted by the people is that when there is unemployment only the out of work are hurt. This is not true. Real economic losses occur for everyone from massive unemployment, affecting the standard of living of all Canadians. Estimates of some of these costs in 1976 show that every 1 per cent of 104,000 unemployed results in a loss of income and output of $2.1 billion, amounting to $20,000 for each unemployed worker. Every 1 per cent reduction in unemployment would have reduced unemployment insurance payments by about $5 million. The government itself lost about $412 billion in tax revenues because of lost income due to unemployment.
The Conference Board of Ottawa, which is a prestigious institution independent of the government, recently reported that Canadians lost $12 billion in income and output last year due to unemployment, amounting to $520 for every man, woman and child in the country. There are many other impor-
November 24, 1977

tant costs of unemployment, such as reduced job security and the pressure to accept lower wages. Another myth frequently repeated is that Canada is pricing itself out of the world market. The truth of the matter is that we are selling more end products or manufactured goods than before. The rate has been increasing. What has been happening is that we are spending more on services such as interest, dividend payments and tourism. It does not make sense to say we are pricing ourselves out of world markets when in fact the volume in end product exports has grown steadily.
We are told that Canada-U.S. wage settlements indicate that our wage settlements are higher than in the U.S.A. These statistics are highly unreliable. United States figures are based on settlements in firms of 20 or more employees, and Canadian settlements on firms of 500 or more employees. Larger firms pay higher wages. It is quite wrong, and contrary to the facts, to blame the workers and say they do not work hard enough. This is simply an irresponsible effort to lay further blame on the workers for our economic problems. No one can dispute that we do have serious economic problems, but the fact remains that the top 20 per cent of Canadians receive 42.5 per cent of total income, and the bottom 20 per cent receive only 4 per cent of total income.
Let us get our priorities straight. The provision of jobs should be our first priority. Unfortunately, experience has shown the government's policy as revealed in the earlier budget and the present mini-budget failed to do this. The emphasis of these budgetary measures is to give incentives to industry, but it is certainly not the fact that these incentives necessarily produce jobs.
Others in this debate will have discussed the situation in the mining industry in northern Ontario in such places as Sudbury and Noranda. I wish to deal with a different sort of industry, but nevertheless an illustration of the same thing. 1 would like to refer to the situation in Northern Telecom Limited. This company is a subsidiary of Bell Telephone and, in effect, is a multinational corporation. The result of the reduction in income tax brought about by the former minister of finance was to produce an effective reduction for this company, in income tax, from 42.8 per cent to 40.6 per cent for the first half of 1977. One would have imagined that if the government's theory had anything to it, these tax concessions to corporations would have resulted in more employment-but the opposite is the truth.
Various unions throughout the country have been notified that Canadian employment by Northern Telecom will be dropped by approximately 2,000 people in the 18 months ending at the end of 1977. More lay-offs are promised after that. For example, a number of employees in the western region installation department will be reduced by about 400 in the last six months of 1977. Early in 1975 there were approximately 2,400 hourly-rated employees in the switching manufacturing plant in Bramalea. By the end of September, 1977, there will be less than 1,200, or half as many.

Other cutbacks have taken place in Montreal. There are quite a number of unions involved: the United Automobile Workers, with a total man-shift of about 3,450; the United Electrical Workers, with 1,200 members in Bramalea; the Communications Workers of Canada, with 1,811 members; the Canadian Union of Communications Workers, with 4,970 members; and the Canadian Office Employees Union, who represent 1,800 office workers in Montreal. All these people are threatened with being laid off.
Northern Telecom, which was formerly Northern Electric, has announced its intention to expand into larger foreign markets and to expand its research development capacity by spreading its operations into the United States. I do not have the details to show the obvious connection of the lay-offs in Canada to the expansion into southern parts of the United States, but it is very clear. Wages in the southern United States are lower, and unions are virtually non-existent.
One cannot say that this company has been unprofitable. In 1972, Northern had sales of $534 million, while in 1976 the figure was $1,112 million. Profits also expanded from $20.1 million to $77.1 million in the same period. Northern has not been without government assistance, although it is not easy to figure out exactly what that assistance was. Since 1970 Northern has had duty remissions of over $1 million. It had deferred taxes in 1976 of $41,321,000, up from $18,814,000 in 1970. It has prospered under a lucrative grants system. The industrial Research and Development Incentives Act prohibits disclosure of disbursements under section 13 of the act. 1 have not the slightest doubt that this company has benefited from this act. There is no doubt that the Export Development Corporation has been providing loan assistance and guarantees totalling $58 million to the company from 1968 to 1973.
In August of this year the corporation announced a $144.5 million loan to Northern to support the manufacture of telephone equipment for a new system in Turkey. So what, in effect, we are doing is subsidizing a large multinational corporation from government funds in various forms which then uses the money to shift employment out of Canada rather than to increase employment in Canada.

I was talking about the loan and saying that what is happening is that we are subsidizing corporations which are then spreading employment to other parts of the world for their own profit, which is reasonable from their point of view, instead of maintaining employment in Canada.

November 24, 1977

I think what is definitely needed is an increase in consumer demand. This could be done by reducing taxes for those earning under $15,000 a year by a one-month moratorium on personal income tax, a further personal income tax reduction and an increase in old age security of $50 a month. With this increased demand existing, savings would be transformed into productive investment.
The government itself must get busy on a job-creation program and a more equitable distribution of income. This is a short-term program of immediate steps. There are no easy solutions for the future well-being and prosperity of Canadians, but there is a necessity for planning in the economy and for the development of a national industrial strategy. We must recognize the right to employment at a living wage as the cornerstone of a productive and equitable society.
Our tax system must be directed at preventing inflation by taxing those who benefit from it. We are not proposing the nationalization of all industries. The private sector will remain, but there is a need for the public sector to act as a balance-wheel to ensure that we use our human and financial resources in a policy of full employment. There are many urgent needs such as housing, better research, day-care centres and recreational facilities. We can afford to have these if we are prepared to plan to use what we have intelligently, and particularly if we are not afraid to rely, at least in part, on the public sector and not solely on the private sector which has demonstrated its inability to maintain an economy of full employment.

I have read that material and I seem to have made a deduction which is different from that made by the hon. parliamentary secretary. I have made the deduction that the result of all these various subsidies has been to assist the company in transferring its activities outside Canada rather than increasing its facilities in Canada. Most of what I have said today has been based on information supplied to me by the workers in these various companies.

Mr. Speaker, what we are discussing today, and what we have been discussing for the past two weeks and more, purports to be simply a bill containing some amendments to the Income Tax Act. In fact, of course, it is nothing other than a mini-budget in disguised form. Why the masquerade, one might ask? The reasons are the same as those for calling the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in October an economic and fiscal statement. It, too, outlined a mini-budget, but the government does not admit it. That is because the government of Canada is reluctant to admit that once again it has been forced to patch up a previous budget which has proved to be inadequate and ill-conceived. In the not too distant future no doubt there will be more piecemeal measures brought in, in order to plug the holes and to correct the inadequacies in the provisions now before us.
If the government is downplaying the fact that this bill is actually budgetary in nature, it is surely because it is ashamed and embarrassed by the unco-ordinated, band-aid approach it has taken to Canada's economic problems-and I can hardly blame it.
Let us take, for example, the proposals regarding the tax treatment of life insurance policies. In the previous budget in March the government proposed to tax, among other things, the cash surrender value of a life insurance policy in excess of the premiums paid at the time of the owner's death. With a grim sense of logic, these proceeds payable at death which exceeded the amount paid into the policy at that point would be considered some sort of taxable gain to the bereaved spouse or children. However, in the face of massive protests, not only by the opposition but also by the public, the government next suggested a modification to this taxation scheme. Now it is proposed that a threshold of $10,000 be placed on the amount of the death benefits to be taxed.
Beside the fact that this in no way affected the unacceptable principle on which this particular tax was founded, it did little to mitigate the hardships it caused, for with the inflation with which we are living today, thanks in large part to the policies of this government over the last many years, this threshold will soon provide little protection. In any event, a threshold does not eliminate the fact that the tax was directed at money which was intended to be an emergency sum or an indemnity against the financial consequences of the premature death of the head of a family.
Now it appears that the government has finally bowed to pressure and proposes to drop this measure. It has taken eight months of outcry by the people of Canada, but it has been done. Yet I have to wonder if this provision was not intended to be withdrawn all along. By introducing an obviously unacceptable proposal such as this, was the government hoping that it would be the focus for protest and that it could then be withdrawn stage by stage as an apparent indication of the government's implied willingness to listen and to compromise? At the same time, however, its purpose would be fulfilled if it could draw attention from related tax proposals which are

speechtext: Order! It being five o'clock, the House will now proceed to private members' business as listed on today's order paper. As there are no notices of motions (papers) listed, the House will proceed to private bills and resume debate on Bill C-1001.

The House resumed, from Thursday, November 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. O'Connell that Bill C-1001, respecting Bell Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Leggatt.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-1001 is legislation respecting Bell Canada introduced by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell). I think all of us should appreciate the hon. member because he was one of the whiz-kids, with Walter Gordon, back in the late sixties when Mr. Gordon ran into difficulties with his budget. Then the hon. member became an elected member in 1968, and from 1968 to 1972 he served as a member of the cabinet, in a very distinguished way, as minister of labour. In 1972 he was defeated.
From October, 1972, until 1974 he served as special adviser to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and was re-elected in 1974. The hon. member is an economist of note. He has made a contribution to Canada in that field. Therefore, we must look closely at Bill C-1001 to see what the hon. member is attempting to do on behalf of Bell Canada. He is attempting to take a private monopoly telephone company outside the control and supervision of parliament concerning changes in the company's objectives and powers. The intention is to make changes by letters patent which would be consistent with the terms of the Canada Corporations Act, the Canada Business Corporations Act and the Telesat Canada Act.
It means, therefore, that any public scrutiny regarding Bell Canada's capital formation, borrowing powers, lending powers, investment powers and ancillary powers will be outside the purview of parliament, and any effects of Bell's telephone restructure will be after the fact and not before the fact. This indicates the importance of Bill C-1001.
Clause 2(14) is the key clause in the bill. It provides, under proposed section 5.3, that Bell will in future be able to alter its objects, powers and capital stock by letters patent. This means that the company will apply to the Minister of Consumer and
Bell Canada
Corporate Affairs for letters patent. If the minister rejects the application it is not appealable. However, if approved, the letters patent are tabled in the House of Commons, and 30 days thereafter they take effect. Members may petition the House objecting to the letters patent and procure a debate. Upon termination of the debate, there is no vote and the minister is not bound to any action on the matter. This is analogous to the Anti-Inflation Board provision whereby a member of parliament may, by petition, bring legislation before the House, have debate and then at the end of the debate no vote is taken. This provision drastically alters the ability of parliament to scrutinize Bell Canada, giving it a free hand to alter its powers and objects.
Under the same clause 2(14) the bill provides inclusion under section 16 of the Canada Corporations Act. This clause allows Bell, ancillary and incidental to its objects set out in letters patent, to exercise any or all of a list of powers, including investment in any business venture, and complete market freedom. This is a regressive step which will provide Bell an incentive to neglect basic telephone service.
Included in the bill is a provision to increase the capitalization from $1.75 billion to $5 million. We, in this House, have experience with banks, insurance companies, oil companies and finance companies and changes in their names, their objects, powers, and so on. The result has been legislation to remove changes in these fields from public scrutiny, and now we have little or no control over the financial and insurance institutions in Canada.
This brings into focus a very important philosophical question-that of public ownership versus private ownership of a public monopoly corporation. Bell Canada is not just another corporation, because only 7 cents of every revenue dollar from the competitive market is obtained from such activities as data transmission services which provide such a vital public service as telephone communication. In other words, out of every $1 earned, 93 cents is obtained from the public monopoly of telephone communication services, and a mere 7 cents from other investments.
We have to look at the philosophy of private and public monopolies, and in that discussion we have to bring into focus and under scrutiny the multinational corporations. Within the last 30 years we have had the public phenomenon of the multinational corporation in different sectors of the Canadian economy. I do not think it is necessary to go into detail about how private monopolies control the resources of Canada and, by doing so, control the production output and the price of services.
The income tax bill presently being debated by the House is ample proof of the benefits obtained from the government by these private monopolies. Need I mention the oil companies, the nickel companies, the aluminium companies who have control over our major resources and whose major thrust is to obtain the greatest profit for their shareholders? I imagine the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Scarborough East who sponsored the bill will ask what is wrong with the large corporations concentrating on
