Bell Canada
profit for shareholders. If this were a private company operating in an ordinary way in a competitive market, that principle might be acceptable. This is a private monopoly of a public enterprise-namely, the telephone system in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and others whose sole concern is to obtain the greatest profit for its shareholders.
We in the New Democratic Party have joined issue with the philosophy of this bill and with members of the Liberal party and the Conservative party to determine whether a corporation that has a monopoly on telephone communications services should have the powers it is attempting to obtain. We feel that the profits they make should not merely be shared with the shareholders, but with the users and should be for the benefit of the general public. That is the very sharp difference between a private monopoly of a public enterprise and a public monopoly of a private enterprise.
We have heard different views expressed on this bill, but members of my party have been unanimous in saying that in a public monopoly of a public enterprise, the greatest benefits should obtain to users and the general public. The public monopoly is not new to members of this House. This is what public enterprise should be all about.
Mr. Speaker, I am interested in ownership, service, rates and the efficiency of a public enterprise. We have in Bell Canada a private company which has complete monopoly of the telephone communications system in the province of Ontario. They operate on the myth that the main shareholders of Bell Canada consist of widows and orphans. Mr. Speaker, I think it is only fair that I bring to your attention just who does own the main shares of Bell Canada, because it is very important that the public know who they are. I wish I could present the tables which I have in front of me with regard to the capital structure of Bell Canada. They show Bell Canada has capital debts in the form of mortgages and bonds, and they have capital stock in the form of common stock and preferred shares-conversion A they are called-preferred shares, conversion C, preferred shares D and E, and so forth. This makes us all appreciate the complexity of corporate law in these operations.
Mr. Speaker, let me read the information on the main shareholders. This information was obtained from the best source possible, namely, the Financial Post survey of funds, 1976. It would take me a great deal of time to list them all, but I will give you a few examples of who, in the main, holds shares in Bell Canada. Principally, they are the insurance companies, the finance companies, the large corporations, Canada Trust RSP, 62,000 common shares, Eaton Commonwealth 50,000 common shares, Confederated Life (Canadian) 63,400 common shares, Great West Life 20,000 common shares, Investors Growth 169,087 common shares, and 320,000 preferred E shares. Then we have Investors Mutual, with 144,225 common shares, Manulife Diversified, 101,200 common shares. In the words of my colleague from Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), "What orphans and widows own the
[Mr. Gilbert.)
shares of Bell Canada"? With regard to the bonds, they are in the names of the National Insurance Company, United Corporations, Provident Mutual Fund, and so forth.
Without doubt, the main ownership of these companies does not lie with widows and orphans; it lies with the large corporations throughout Canada. You have probably heard, Mr. Speaker, the clever advertising Bell Canada has on television. I wish I could sing it. It goes someing like this, "If your're feeling lonely, if you're feeling blue, just pick up the phone and call long distance." When I read the list of ownership of Bell Canada shares and bonds, I felt a little bit lonely and a little bit blue, because 1 realize that the ownership is not with the widows and the orphans, but with the large corporations.
Who did you telephone?

Mr. Speaker, I could not telephone anyone. This is the unfortunate part, because if you cannot telephone someone you have a duty to get up in the House to speak and tell the Canadian public that you have concern with regard to the widows and the orphans and you want to make sure that they are taken care of. I do not like to have that myth perpetrated by Bell Canada with respect to its ownership being in the hands of widows and orphans.
I have read the speeches of my colleagues with regard to the service and, more especially, the non-urban service. When I read the speeches of the members for Sault Ste. Marie and Nickel Belt, I realized people in the non-urban areas suffered greatly with regard to telephone service. Within 25 miles of Sault Ste. Marie, people cannot get service. Within a short distance of the Nickel Belt area, people, if they desire service, have to pay tremendous rates and tremendous service charges even to have the telephone installed. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the main thrust of any public corporation should be that the profits are used for the benefit of the users and for the service of the community at large.
We have heard a great deal with regard to rates. I think it would be fair to say that the rates in Ontario, under a private corporation such as Bell Canada, are higher than Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia. The evidence by my colleagues has shown that the rates to private users have been much lower. So, too, have the commercial rates. I thought the member from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), had a point with respect to the difficulties corporations have concerning services in the large urban centres and the amounts of money that is required. That leads me to the simple proposition, if that is the case, that all the profits-or most of the profits-which are obtained should be put into the service of these people rather than into the pockets of the shareholders of these large corporations. If time permits, I would like to place on record a statement that a competitor of Bell Canada is accused of overcharging in the United States. It is an article by UPI, dated March 28 which says:
Bell Telephone may be overcharging home and business telephone users in the U.S. more than $2.2 billion yearly to finance a war on competition, a Bell competitor said Sunday.
November 24, 1977

Edwin Spievack, general counsel for the North American Telephone Association, which represents 400 independent telephone equipment manufacturers, said the overcharge averages about $20 a year for every main telephone subscriber in the nation.
I wish I had time to develop more of this, Mr. Speaker, but you can see why we, in the New Democratic Party, are opposed to this bill.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-1001. According to the mover of the bill, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), Bill C-1001 has four objects. First, to increase the present limit of the authorized capital stock from $1,750,000 to $5 million; second, to give more financial flexibility to Bell Canada so that it may adjust itself to the changes which can occur in the economy and on the capital market; third, to modernize the administrative powers of the company; the purpose of this bill is to elucidate and broaden its real and ancillary powers; fourth, to give the company the authority to alter from now on by letters patent the company's objects, powers and capital stock.
The charter of Bell Canada was granted under a legislation of Parliament. Any change to that charter must be approved by the people's representatives, that is Parliament. This bill would practically remove any control of Parliament over that company. The letters patent process theoretically gives a power of decision to Parliament, but it really removes that power. The application of clause 16 of the Canada Corporations Act, as requested in clause 5(b) of Bill C-1001, would finally enable Bell Canada to launch all kinds of commercial ventures unrelated to communications, because we must remember that we have always been under the impression that Bell Canada was first and foremost a communication corporation, but Bill C-1001 would enable it to enter into all kinds of other fields, to establish other subsidiaries, in addition to those it has already set up.
Bell Canada is a private enterprise providing an essential service to Canadians because it is a monopoly. Parliament should not surrender its right to control the decisions made by this company. If this government allows and even promotes monopolies, it should at least retain the necessary powers to keep a very strict control over them. When we look at the profits they make, we are always astonished to find that the board regulating prices and incomes has not reduced by even one cent the super revenues of all these monopolies in Canada. All this board has done, as we have said in this House, is to control worker's wages, but never these large monopolies' profits.
The net revenues of Bell Canada for the first semester of 1977 over those of 1976 went down from $149 million to $129 million, that is 18 per cent. But this reduction stems from fewer long distance telephone calls due to the very high rates.
Bell Canada
Furthermore, the last rate increases came into force only at the end of the first semester. Therefore revenues for the second semester should be higher due to the new rates.
As it is impossible to obtain figures concerning the profits of the subsidiaries, the true financial situation of these companies remain unknown. The umbrella under which they are hiding distorts realities, so that we can never-neither can the smartest accountant-state for sure what benefits Bell Canada made in any given year, especially because of its relationship with its subsidiaries. The rates of increase are reported to have been 7.8, 18.8, 12.2, 13.3 and 16.6 per cent in 1975, 1974, 1973 and 1972 respectively. But it is when we turn our attention to its subsidiaries that we are in for a big surprise, Mr. Speaker. The rate of increase in net benefits of Northern Telecom Ltd. was 5 per cent in 1976, but it reached 32 per cent in 1975, 62 per cent in 1974 and 60 per cent in 1973. Of course, the profits of the Northern Telecom Co. Ltd. will remain unknown because it is a subsidiary which is 69 per cent owned by Bell Canada.
Here are further statistical data and information, Mr. Speaker. Before 1971, Bell Canada was publishing its own directories. This activity was highly profitable, because of the publicity in the yellow pages. In 1971, Bell Canada created a new subsidiary, Tele Direct Ltd., in which it invested some $9 million to look after the publication of telephone directories. In 1976, this subsidiary's income reached $91 million. That is not too bad.
For an investment of $9 million, nice revenues of $91 million-an investment return of about 75 per cent. Maintenance, traffic and amortizing expenses go up 8 per cent a year. But other expenses have gone up 70 per cent during the last five years. What are those expenses, Mr. Speaker? Now that is an interesting question. Those expenses relate to senior management, legal advisers, public relations, consultant office, rent, various taxes and so on.
For instance, former board chairman Robert Scrivener was paid $201,000 in 1976. When he left Bell Canada to join Northern TTelecom, a subsidiary of Bell, he was given a lump sum of $575,000 and he will draw a pension of $81,000 a year. That is more than the Prime Minister of Canada earns, Mr. Speaker.
This does not take into account the fact that Mr. Scrivener will earn $175,000 with Northern Telecom Limited, Mr. Speaker. I think that instead of appointing some of its friends to the Senate, the Liberal party should send them to this company. It pays more money. Moreover, Mr. Scrivener will receive a pension. A salary of $175,000 is not enough, he will receive a pension. As for the former chairman of Northern Telecom, the American John C. Lobb, he is assured of a pension of $147,000 for ten years. He will also receive $30,000 a year as adviser to the company.
In an interview given to the Ottawa Citizen on October 12, the chairman of Bell Northern Research, another Bell subsidiary, for there are many of them, said that his company was preparing to expand outside Canada rather than over here.

November 24, 1977
Bell Canada
Mr. Speaker, this is the danger that I mentioned at the beginning, the danger that results from the change provided in this bill. Bell Canada, not satisfied with its income and after having made the largest profits in Canada, will take this money to do business in another country. We say that capital is leaving the country, but we are contributing to this with the bill that will be passed today. We are helping Bell Canada to invest in other countries.
In the United States, the Federal Communications Commission has forced American Telephone & Telegraph to stop the multiplication and incestuous union of its subsidiaries. In addition, AT&T will have to submit each year a detailed financial statement for each service it provides. This will provide information on the cost of services and on the returns of the company. The company will no longer be able to make across the board rate increases and will have to restrict increases to the areas where costs make this necessary, which is very vague, Mr. Speaker, and leaves the door wide open to the company. If its returns are too large for one service, it will even have to reduce the rates for this service.
Bell Northern Research has virtually forced into bankruptcy all Canadian manufacturers of coaxial cables, the type of cables which are used in cable TV distribution. Bell no longer manufactures this type of cable and Canadian users have to import them from the United States because Bell Northern got rid of all Canadian competitors. And now Northern Telecom is laying off 1,000 Canadian workers. The increased powers Bell is asking for would give it the power to invest in nearly every field and every country. We can rightfully wonder whether Canadian users, through their phone bills, would not be financing investments which finally would be of no use to them.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-1001, which is being sponsored by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), in my opinion is unacceptable on a number of grounds. My main objection to this bill lies in the fact that it will enable Bell Canada to be removed from the scrutiny of this parliament for many years to come. By asking this parliament to agree to increase their capitalization from $1% billion to $5 billion, it means that in all likelihood there is not a single member of this parliament who will ever see that bill come back for review.
One of the reasons for making provisions in these private bills with respect to capitalization was to ensure that when a company wanted to enlarge its capitalization it would be required to come back to parliament, and members of this House would be able to scrutinize whether or not that particular company operated in the public interest. However, if this House agrees to increase the capitalization from $1 % billion to $5 billion, Bell Canada will go scot free for many, many years to come.
Someone may ask why should there be periodic scrutiny of the operations of Bell Canada. Mr. Speaker, I think it is

speechtext: That is not what Stephen I Lewis says. You better straighten him out.	I

The	I
TVA Tennessee Valley Authority-in the United States,	I
set up under President Roosevelt, has provided the American	I
people with cheap, accessible electric power. It has been of	I
tremendous value to the people of America.	I
In the province of British Columbia governments there, which do fight elections against public ownership of electric utilities, took them over and operated them under public ownership. The government took over the ferry service, and the ferry service is operated by the government of British Columbia. This is not because the governments, which happened to be Social Credit governments, were wedded to socialism, but because they recognized that, in fairness to the consumer, services such as the generation and distribution of
November 24, 1977

electric power, and ferry services, absolutely essential to the people who live on the coastal islands of British Columbia, had to be operated under public ownership in order to protect consumers. That is the danger of leaving a natural monopoly in the hands of a group of individuals who naturally seek to maximize their profit at the expense of consumers. There is no doubt that the consumer is victimized where there is no adequate public protection.
I know it will be argued that in the case of the telephone companies they must apply to the CRTC for increases in their rates. The fact of the matter is that such an application, originally to the CTC and later to the CRTC, has become a farce. These companies are able to hide a good bit of their profits. Bell Telephone, for instance, owns Northern Electric from which it buys its supplies. It can quite well afford to pay inflated prices for its supplies to its own subsidiary, which keeps the profits of the parent company down, and simply transfers them to the subsidiary, Northern Electric.
There are scores of ways by which it is possible for a monopoly such as Bell Telephone to come before a government board and demonstrate that their profit margin is not excessive and that, therefore, they are entitled to a further increase in rates. In fact they have obtained an increase in rates year after year after year.
The fact of the matter is that the services which they have provided in many cases have not warranted the kind of increases they have obtained. I have a letter on my desk right now from a man who complains that while the rates of the telephone company were increased on the grounds that it needed greater capitalization in order to improve the service, in his case, my correspondent claims, the service has not improved at all but has steadily deteriorated. He has sent me copies of the letters he has written to the telephone company complaining about the fact that his service has deteriorated in spite of increasing rates, and in spite of alleged increases in capitalization.
The consumer is being ripped off by virtue of the fact that he has no protection whatsoever against a natural monopoly. If the consumer could purchase goods or services on a competitive basis he could go to another firm, but you cannot go to another telephone company, you cannot go to another power company, and you cannot go to another gas distribution company. They are monopolies.
It is abundantly clear that the monopoly, in this case Bell Telephone Company, has taken advantage of its preferred position. One has only to look at a comparison of rates between the privately owned telephone companies and the rates charged by the publicly owned telephone companies in the three prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta.
When we last discussed this the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) sought to make a case for these higher rates by Bell Telephone Company over the private telephone company rates on the ground that they were serving large cities such as Toronto and Montreal. His argument was that serving a city cost a great deal more money because a
Bell Canada
company has to put in switching operations with many people to service and, consequently, the rates ought to be higher in a large city. He suggested it was unfair to make the kind of comparison my colleagues have been making of rates charged by private telephone companies and those charged by public telephone companies.
Let me say to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that I had close association for some 17 years with the workings of the Saskatchewan Telephone Company, and I know that company was always much more pleased to get an increase in business in the cities than in the small towns and rural areas because it was much less costly to put in additional lines in the city than it was to take telephone lines out into the rural communities and to put up switch boards to serve only a few hundred customers. This is much more expensive than to put in switch boards to serve a more concentrated urban centre.
Even if we accept the argument of the hon. member, and this much of his argument is true, the people in large cities should pay higher rates than the people in small rural areas for the obvious reason that if you live in a city where there are a million telephones, there are a great many more people whom you can telephone from your own house than if you live in a community where there are only 500 telephones. In other words, you are getting a much greater service.
How many of us would call 500 people?

Perhaps people would not make phone calls to 500 different locations in a large city, but the people in the city can make phone calls which would be long distance calls if they lived in a small community, and the hon. member should recognize that fact. That is elementary, even to one with the normal Liberal intellectual capacity.
Even if we accept the argument of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, that it costs more to provide services in a large city, let us take a look to see what happens in comparable areas. For instance, in the city of Calgary, where the public telephone system operates, there are 200,650 telephones. The residential rate is $5.70 and the business rate is $14.70. Let us consider the city of Quebec, which is not very much larger, there being 245,806 telephones, and the rate is $6.55 for residential and $18.70 for a business phone. That is a difference of $4 a month or $48 a year more in Quebec than in Calgary. Let us consider the city of Winnipeg which has about the same number of phones as Quebec City, namely, 237,500. The residential rate there is $4.90, with the business rate being $11.65.
If you consider London, Ontario, which has only 119,483 telephones, by the logic of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre the service ought to cost much less than service to the people in the city of Calgary. However, we find that in London, Ontario, the residential rate is $6.20, which is 50 cents a month more or $6 a year more than in the larger city of Calgary. The business telephone rate is $17 or $2.30 a month more than the business telephone rate in the city of

Bell Canada
Calgary. A businessman in the city of London is paying $27.60 more each year, despite the fact the number of telephones there is a little more than half the number of telephones in the city of Calgary.
How can my friend argue that the reason the private telephone companies have to charge higher rates is because they serve larger centres of population? Even in London, Ontario, where the number of people served is only a little better than half what it is in Calgary, the people in Calgary are getting much lower rates for their residential and business telephones.
I should like to refer to two communities which are almost comparable. The city of Regina has 72,400 telephones, and the residential rate is $5 and the business rate is $11.85. The city of Moncton has 52,200 telephones or 20,000 less telephones. Its residential rate is $7.65 or $2.65 more per month. The rate for a business telephone in Moncton is $22.30 or almost twice what the people in Regina pay, even though there are 20,000 more telephones there.
The city of Edmonton has 207,700 telephones. The residential telephone rate is $5.80, and the business telephone rate is $17. The city of Victoria, which is smaller, has 192,796 telephones. The residential rate there is $6.65, and the business rate is $17.15. By the logic of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, subscribers in Victoria should be paying less, but they are paying more.
In Halifax with 96,249 telephones, the residential rate is $8.95 or $3.15 more than in Edmonton which has twice the population. The business telephone rate is $26, which is $9 more than in Edmonton.
Saint John, New Brunswick has 47,007 telephones. Their residential rate is $7.65, and their business rate is $22.30, which is $5 more than what is charged in the city of Edmonton where there are 2Vi times as many telephones. Certainly that defeats the logic of the argument that the reason the private telephone companies are charging high rates is because they are serving larger centres. By any standard of comparison it is perfectly clear that the people served by these private companies are being ripped off. Not only are they paying more for their telephone service, they are getting a lower quality of service from these private companies.
I sum up by saying that the only way this parliament can protect the telephone users is by defeating this legislation, or so changing it that these companies will be required to come back periodically to parliament in order for parliament to have an opportunity to scrutinize their operations and ensure that Canadian consumers are protected.
I have other objections to some of the clauses in the bill, but perhaps I will have a chance to discuss them at a later date.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that it is two or three minutes before six

o'clock, in a preliminary way I want to say I am happy to join my colleagues in opposition to this bill. This is not the first time we have been faced with this legislation, so our unanimous opposition to it is of no surprise to other members of the House. We do not feel lonely, because there are tens of thousands of Bell Canada subscribers across Canada who are cheering us on, and are happy that once in a blue moon their cause is put before the public and in parliament. The consumers' side must be heard, rather than just hearing about poor Mother Bell who needs another $3*/2 million for capitalization.
The bill goes beyond the stated objective. It is an attempt to exempt Bell Canada from regulation. The telephone service, light, power and natural gas are just too essential to be left to the whims and the tender mercies of private corporations responsible to no one but their shareholders. The objective of these private corporations is to maximize the profits and returns to the shareholders. That is their primary objective. The top priority of private corporations is to make money and not to provide a service. With that lack of social conscience or moral treatment of the communities those companies serve, no one can blame their subscribers for protesting this kind of legislation.
Treating telephone service as a public utility is not only logical, it should be obvious to anyone. Because it is a public utility that is privately owned, minimum regulations apply to Bell Canada's rates of return, assets, and the price it can charge for its services. I would go further with respect to its accountability to the public and its customers by saying that there should be a full scrutiny of the methods of operation used by Bell Canada, their labour management relations, the way they spend their money, and how generous they are to the board of directors.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-POSSIBILITY OF PUBLIC HEARINGS ON PROPOSAL TO INCREASE TOLLS
TRANSPORT-ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-POSSIBILITY OF PUBLIC HEARINGS ON PROPOSAL TO INCREASE TOLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about the minister's answer to a question I asked last week in the House concerning the gross increase in Seaway tolls.
Canadian users have not been given the opportunity of public hearings that American users have been given to discuss
November 24, 1977

these increases. This is particularly galling to Canadian users since they represent 70 per cent of the tonnage and pay about 63 per cent of the tolls. These Canadian users who are concerned, such as people in the grain industry, ship owners, unions dealing with grain handling, seamen, farmers, various business groups, chambers of commerce, and so on, are very concerned.
Certainly ship owners are not concerned for themselves particularly because they know they will be able to absorb the extra cost, but they are concerned about the loss in business which they believe could very well occur, and also the loss of jobs. Basically they are concerned with the size of the increase-the cost will be approximately doubled-and with the suddenness of the increase. They believe this could create some very bad psychological effects. For instance, it could create a diversion of ore from Sept-Isles to Philadelphia or Baltimore. This would mean that the cost of moving grain would be considerably higher since grain from western ports moves east and the ore traditionally moves back. We could have an increase in cost for the movement of grain, if ships came back empty, of 4 cents or 5 cents a bushel.
They are also concerned about the diversion of grain to the Pacific coast. They are concerned, too, about unit trains which, given the increased tolls, might by-pass Thunder Bay and move grain to east coast ports. They are also concerned about loss of sales.
The Seaway Authority says the increase will cost only an extra cent a bushel, but when grain is sold in quarter cent quotes per bushel and quotes are made at $2.9514, 1 cent is a large sum and, if a ship comes back empty, 4 cents or 5 cents is a sum which could result in serious losses.
The Seaway stands to gain something in the order of $22 million. The users, people working on the Seaway, are concerned they could lose $70 million to $100 million with an attendant loss of jobs.
One of the things that concerns me is whether or not the Authority actually needs the amount of money it says it needs. The deficit this year was $6.5 million, with depreciation added of $1.2 million, and with the new policy of the 1 per cent tax on the $625 million debt on the Seaway, the total amount would come to $14 million. If you add 7 per cent or 8 per cent for inflation, you are talking in terms of about $15 million. The Seaway authority is talking in terms of picking up between $20 million and $22 million.
If the minister were to take another look at this and allow for some public hearings, either through the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications or through some independent body, and think in terms of these increases over three to five years, spreading them over a longer period of time and not creating the psychological situation which may cause this diversion, the users, my constituents, and people who live along the Seaway would be a great deal happier.
I am opposed to this move because I am afraid we will lose considerable business, but I am also opposed to it on other
Adjournment Debate
grounds, namely, that this is a move in the direction of the user-pay concept. I think the user-pay policy is not a policy which will satisfy the needs of Canadians. It is a policy which tends to favour the inner core of the country, the Golden Horseshoe, but it certainly does nothing for people in the Atlantic provinces, northern Ontario, or in the west. The user-pay principle is one about which I am very concerned. I think it will bring disunity to the country. For these reasons I oppose both the size and the suddenness of these increases, and I hope the minister will reconsider his stand on this matter and allow open hearings to take place.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) just made can easily be understood, and the member was of course making himself the spokesman for the St. Lawrence Seaway users who of course are not happy to face a toll increase. It is quite normal for any user of a service not to be fully happy when an increase is announced. However, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) does not intend to refer the question of higher tolls for transit in the St. Lawrence Seaway to the House Standing Committee on Transport nor to any other body.
The Seaway authorities have stated for several years the need for a toll increase to stop the accumulating and ever increasing yearly deficits in spite of the fact that tonnage is going up as well. I was nevertheless surprised to hear the hon. member say that this is a sudden increase. If my records are correct, I believe the succeeding governments have asked for and talked about an increase in the seaway tolls since 1964. The Minister of Transport himself has repeatedly and publicly announced that he intended to recommend higher tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway. All people directly concerned have closely followed the negotiations that have taken place between our government and that of the United States. Those people, on both sides of the border, have had the full opportunity to express their opinions and justify their objections and they have not missed the occasion to do so that the negotiations between the two countries provided them with. Public audiences would not have been more advantageous to them than the meetings they have had with the authorities of the St. Lawrence Seaway, the Marine Administration of the department or the minister himself.
As I was saying at the beginning of my reply, it is no surprise that the users of the seaway object to an increase in their transportation costs since people never welcome an increase in their costs. The fact remains that current tolls have not changed since 1959 and that the increases which the governments of the two countries associated in the St. Lawrence Seaway now propose will not even bring the tolls back to the level that had been deemed acceptable in 1959. I think this partially answers the objection that the rate of increase is too high. These tolls have not changed for nearly twenty years now and it seems reasonable to me that they be readjusted, given

subtopic: ENERGY-URANIUM-REASON GOVERNMENT AQUIESCED IN CARTEL ARRANGEMENT
ENERGY-URANIUM-REASON GOVERNMENT AQUIESCED IN CARTEL ARRANGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter which brings me into the adjournment debate this evening is the international uranium cartel, and particularly the effect this possibly illegal cartel will have on prices Canadians will pay in the future for electricity.
On Monday last I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) about a contract a cartel member, Gulf Minerals Canada Limited, signed with Ontario Hydro in 1974, apparently with the blessing of the federal government. Gulfs own records on this deal now reveal for the first time that Gulf charged the consumers of Ontario, prices which were in line-in fact, dead on-with cartel prices set by the Club of Five in Paris. These records of Gulf boast of the profit Gulf will make on the deal, some $50 million at least, on a contract valued by Gulf at $98 million.
These records point proudly to the fact that by virtue of its membership in the cartel, which was sponsored by the Canadian government, Gulf was charging Ontario Hydro prices far in excess of the going world market price. 1 would like to quote from a Gulf memo dated March 8, 1974, referring specifically to the Hydro contract to which I have just made reference. The memo states, and I quote:
The above prices are considerably higher than either the current world market price or the latest prices established by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources as being the minimum for export of Canadian uranium.
What is worse, Mr. Speaker, the government appears to have known of and even approved this contract which we now know to be based on prices rigged in Paris by the cartel. Again referring specifically to the Hydro contract the above cited memo says:
The EMR staff does however recognize that Canadian utilities must be prepared to pay the same prices that we could achieve from export sales.
In 1974, Mr. Speaker, export prices were one and the same as cartel prices.
Another document, dated February 26, 1976, raises even more serious questions. This memo hints darkly that the government even went so far as to offer Gulf "protection from government action," meaning, I suspect, protection from legal action. It says:
At the time the (Hydro) proposal was made $12.50 plus 90 per cent escalation plus protection from government action was at the top of the market.
When I asked the minister why his department-contrary to repeated public statements-allowed a cartel member to charge cartel prices in Canada, the minister hedged the question, suggesting I was an "agent for a foreign corporation."
Frankly, the real question is, who is the minister acting for in this matter? Is he acting on behalf of Canadian consumers

who are going to be using electricity, or is he acting for certain rather secret interests, certain foreign corporations such as Gulf U.S. or Rio Algom. Incidentally, the Gulf operation is estimated by them to yield between $3 million and $3'/2 million per year after tax profits for as long as the deal continues.
The real question in my mind is whether the minister is more concerned with Ontario users of electricity or with saving members of his government from embarrassment.
Frankly, his answers look pretty fishy. When I asked the minister if he has reviewed the Hydro contract he said in effect, "Why should I? Ontario Hydro hasn't complained!" Mr. Speaker, that is just not true. I should like to read into the record a few comments Hydro made at the time the cartel was forcing Canadians, including Hydro, to pay rigged prices for uranium.
Minutes of a meeting of the Ontario Hydro finance committee on July 15, 1974, report:
Uranium suppliers have clearly indicated that uranium prices will be equated to the so-called "World Price" calculated at or near to the year of delivery.
"World price" was the term the cartel used to describe cartel prices in 1974. The report concludes that, under present circumstances, Hydro does not have a strong bargaining position and may have to pay world market prices even though they will lead to significantly high uranium costs.
I am sorry the minister is not with us tonight, Mr. Speaker. I hope he will stop stonewalling this whole cartel misadventure, particularly this contract with Hydro. I hope he will tell us why the government permitted the people of Ontario to be ripped off by a cartel member.
I think it is time the government started to answer a few questions on this entire affair. Certain blind or frozen trusts that have been reported at the time the cartel was established have to be opened up and explained. Do these blind trusts include members or former members of the Government of Canada, for example? These are questions that have to be asked. To use the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) expression, "It looks fishy." I think it is time questions were answered instead of being stonewalled as we were last Monday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to repeat, for the benefit of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the details concerning the marketing of uranium. From August 17, 1972 to March 6, 1974, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) issued five directives on price fixing to the Chairman of the Atomic Energy Control Board. Another one issued on March 27, 1975 invalidated all former directives. All relevant details are given in a press release dated October 14, 1977.

It had become clear by early 1974 that there had been a dramatic turn-around in the uranium market from a buyer's
November 24, 1977

market to a seller's one. After many years of relative inactivity, Canadian uranium marketing personnel found themselves with far more inquiries than could be accommodated. Hence, during the first six months of 1974, the Canadian uranium industry contracted for sale into the export market, for future years, a total of 45,000 tons of uranium oxide, some ten times the then Canadian annual production rate.
The government, recognizing that the market had switched so positively, moved to ensure that domestic uranium consumers would not be caught in the position of not having enough future uranium supplies from domestic sources to satisfy their own nuclear power programs. This was a very real risk in mid 1974. As a result, on September 5, 1974, the government announced a uranium export policy which protects domestic utilities with long term assured supplies through the creation of a system to establish domestic reserve allocations. It is not surprising, therefore, that by March, 1975, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources felt that it was no longer necessary to specify a minimum price for uranium sales in order to protect against what had pertained in earlier years, namely, that uranium mines were being high-graded and sales were sometimes made at prices below operating costs in order to prevent mine shutdowns.
In the last pricing direction issued on March 6, 1974, the minimum price specified for sale of uranium from Canada was $8.20 per pound, for delivery in 1974; $9.05 in 1975; $10.00 in 1976; $11.05 in 1977, and $12.20 in 1978. For deliveries during the period 1979 through 1985 or, as an alternative to the minimum fixed price schedule just mentioned, escalated prices on a base price of $9.70 per pound could be offered. The escalation formula was to operate from 1974 at the stipulated base price, irrespective of the first delivery year in the contract. At least 80 per cent of the price was to be subject to escalation, and the labour and materials cost components of the escalation formula were to be at least 30 per cent each.
In the direction of March 6, 1974, as in all previous pricing directions, it was made clear that the Canadian market was to be excluded.

ENERGY-OIL-SUGGESTED SHORTAGE BY MID-1980's-REQUEST FOR INCREASED COAL PRODUCTION IN NOVA SCOTIA

subtopic: ENERGY-URANIUM-REASON GOVERNMENT AQUIESCED IN CARTEL ARRANGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has been repeating for the last few months that Canada faces the threat of a serious energy crisis in the mid 1980's. The minister recently, in early November, told a Toronto audience that even if people do not see it, it is like the iceberg that sank the Titanic. Again, in response to my question in the House today, he repeated his serious concern that Canada ceased to be self-sufficient in oil last year.
The minister has committed Canada to a target of imports of no more than 800,000 barrels a day by 1985, which would still cost over $4 billion a year. Paying for this imported oil is only one part of the problem, although an extremely difficult one. In addition, it is going to become increasingly difficult to ensure that there is enough oil to buy at any price, although experts disagree on timing. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology study, the Central Intelligence Agency study of supply and demand for world oil, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, as well as the leaders of the organization of petroleum exporting countries-which control most of the oil-all have warned that sometime in the 1980's there will not be enough oil in the world to go around, even if we use rigorous conservation practices.
The head of Petroleos de Venezuela recently said in Toronto:
... in ten years the surplus oil production capacity of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) will gradually disappear as demand rises and additional supplies of oil from outside the OPEC area are not forthcoming in significant quantities ... When this happens, international crude oil prices will again rise steeply, perhaps to as much as $20 a barrel in 1976 dollars.
The Cape Breton oil industry is now at a point at which it can make a contribution to the balance of payments problem of our country if the federal government will quickly start two new deep mines, as well as using some of the coal that can be stripped in that area for Nova Scotia's own power needs, such as at the new generating plant being built at Lingan, outside New Waterford, Nova Scotia.
Over and above what we can supply for ourselves in Nova Scotia, there is a market which was formerly held by the Cape Breton coal industry when it was under private ownership but which was lost during the era of cheap, imported oil, which has now come to an end. I refer to the heavy industries in the southern part of Quebec, such as cement, pulp and paper, iron and titanium, and many others which are now using the very expensive imported heavy oil. For example, last year in 1976

November 24, 1977
Adjournment Debate
there were 41.3 million barrels of heavy oil imported into Quebec at 35 imperial gallons per barrel. The forest products industries use 24 per cent of this volume; cement and smaller industries use another 20 per cent; mining, smelting, and quarries use 12 per cent, and marine industries use 13 per cent.
The best targets for Cape Breton coal to substitute for some of the industrial users of heavy imported oil are the major pulp and paper and cement plants, etc. which are situated on or near St. Lawrence ports and can be readily reached by water shipment from Sydney Harbour. Practically all these industries used coal until the late 1950's and their steam plants or cement kilns can again use coal after reconversion to coal firing apparatus. Now it takes about four barrels of this heavy oil imported into Quebec to be equal in British thermal units of heat value to one ton of coal, so one can easily see that Government of Canada could, for an investment in a new coal mine in Cape Breton, help immensely these industries in Quebec to survive competitively and, as I mentioned before, this would in turn help Canada's balance of payments.
There is one major fly in the ointment, so to speak. The industries I have mentioned would have to reconvert their steam boiler plants, or cement kilns, from oil to coal firing at substantial capital cost. This involves not only the boilers but also the reconversion of their coal storage grounds. Given the concern in our day for pollution control, modern devices to reduce fly ash and noxious gases from their stacks would be needed.
It would appear to be economically beneficial for the Government of Canada and or Quebec to allow such companies a form of tax forgiveness or fast write-off for their coal conversion costs. On the Cape Breton side, from Devco's point of view, the corporation would have to reconstruct the customer contacts the former private owners of the Cape Breton coal mines had with these industries in Quebec and re-establish a coal flow marketing system in the St. Lawrence trade. None of this can be done overnight, but it is imperative that these problems be tackled as soon as possible.
It is obvious that the future supply of energy is a serious corporate concern to all these Quebec industries. Currently they depend almost entirely, as I said before, on imported oil. These industries, to repeat, are concerned not only with the sharply rising price of oil but also and, more significantly, with the future uncertainty of the supply itself. This is particularly true with respect to the additional supplies of oil required for normal industrial expansion. The uncertainty, unless corrected, will place a marked restriction on normal industrial growth in the province of Quebec.
There is a market opportunity for three to four million tons of thermal coal on the St. Lawrence waterway of Quebec province. The question is, can and will Cape Breton be prepared to supply that important profitable market? It is my opinion that the Cape Breton coal fields can, with expansion, provide at least a million tons of coal per year, and perhaps two million tons, which would be over and above Nova Scotia's own needs. What is required is a genuine co-operative effort by the federal government, Quebec industry, and Devco to estab-

lish a market development strategy conducted in orderly coordination with a mine expansion program in the Sydney coal fields. It is obvious that time is pressing, both for Cape Breton and Quebec, and serious planning must not suffer from procrastination from any quarter.

Those activities are undertaken in co-operation with Nova Scotia, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, Devco, the Treasury Board and they are aimed at reducing Canadian dependence on imported oil, particularly in the Maritimes.

These co-operative activities embrace all aspects of coal development and utilization.
As far as exploration is concerned, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is providing technical advice to DREE for the coal drilling program currently being conducted both onshore and offshore in Nova Scotia. The cumulative expenditure on this program amounts to about $8 million, of which 80 per cent, or $6.4 million, is contributed by DREE.
As far as mining is concerned, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, as a federal Crown corporation, has been completely modernized and now operates two new mines, one rehabilitated mine, and a new preparation plant. In addition to the capital requirements, Treasury Board approved a substantial grant of $28 million last year to cover the deficit in operations.
As for utilization, under the Canada-Nova Scotia agreement on oil substitution and conservation, which is administered federally by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, $9 million has been made available directly, and a further $15 million will be available through loans for, among other things, accelerating the construction of new coal-fired power plants and experiments in combustion of coal-oil slurries in existing oil fired plants.

However, the new mines can be established only when the results of the exploration have been evaluated, the economic effects of foreign oil substitution by national coal have been measured and experimental combustion has been made.
I hope that with this additional information all hon. members and all those who are listening to us will appreciate the efforts and the constructive and co-operative approach implemented by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to reduce the dependency of Cape Breton, Nova Scotia and the Maritimes as concerns imported oil. And this is the objective at which we continually aim in the interest of every Canadian.
November 24, 1977

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-ll, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner hour 1 was addressing a few remarks to the provisions of the bill before us as they relate to the treatment of insurance policies. Now I should like to examine the other proposals relating to insurance policies, one of which concerns loans taken by policyholders against their life insurance policies.
The Department of Revenue proposes to have the amount of the loan that exceeds the value of premiums paid, to be added to the borrower's income. In other words, the gain portion of the loan is to be treated as an advance or disposition, and is to be taxed as such. This suggestion attacks the concept of paid up insurance constituting tangible property. While money borrowed on the security of real estate is not taxable, these measures insist that borrowing on the security of the paid up portion of an insurance policy does not warrant similar consideration. This is clearly unjust. A policy loan should be regarded as just that, because the loan is ultimately repayable out of the insurance proceeds, if it has not been repaid earlier.
In introducing this measure the government is effectively eliminating a ready source of low interest loans, easily accessible to finance such projects as sending a child to college, paying uninsured medical expenses, or effecting household improvements.
Traditionally and historically, policy loan provisions have constituted well established and valuable features of life insurance programs in Canada. Changing the rules in mid-stream, as the minister proposes, will further erode the incentive to
Income Tax
save and provide for one's own future, which at one time was a significant feature of the Canadian style of family life.
Many, if not all, current policy owners bought their policies in the expectation that in times of financial need or emergency they could borrow against their policies without being taxed. To change this provision is to undermine a basic feature of life insurance policies. In so far as this provision was simply intended to plug a possible loophole for avoiding the now defunct proposal for a tax at death, it is clearly pointless.
A third proposed measure regarding life insurance policy owners would disallow the deduction of interest on policy loans designed to be utilized in such a way as to increase the policy owner's income. An example of this might be a small businessman borrowing against his policy to improve his business. This proposal will serve only to further hamper access by small business to low cost financing, and place a further burden on the private sector of our economy. It should be recognized that life insurance policies are often the best, if not the only, source of ready cash for small business operators, since money can be obtained quickly at modest rates with no questions asked and no further collateral demanded.
In addition to the foregoing, the proposed measures regarding life insurance would have the effect of greatly increasing the administrative burden for insurers by the additional record keeping and reporting for ordinary policy loans, automatic premium loans, and payments of interest, thereby adding to the cost of insurance to the public. However, we should not be so surprised that the major effect of government tax amendments seems to be to raise prices, for the primary objective of these amendments appears to make the law, as it relates to income tax, even more tortuous and convoluted than it is already.
This bill that we are discussing today is nearly an inch thick, and all of 200 pages long. This is in addition to the 424 pages of the 1970 revised version of the Income Tax Act, and the hundreds of pages of amending acts between that date and this. Many of the amendments and obfuscations of income tax laws are the offspring of the "equity in taxation" hobbyhorse that is being ridden by senior advisers down the corridors of the Department of Finance. No one would claim the major inequities that existed in the tax system of days gone by should not have been eliminated, but we are at the point now where small and almost meaningless discrepancies in fairness are being operated upon to the over-all detriment of the system.
Let us consider one of the changes proposed in the bill-the provision to tax interest free loans to employees and shareholders. It is a purely equity based amendment. However, the consequence will be untold man-hours poured into revising compensation packages and looking for ways to circumvent the application of the rule, hours that undoubtedly could be put to more productive use.
This amendment will raise no revenue; will hurt, not help the economy; and will be nothing but trouble and aggravation to those who will have to enforce it. It is an amendment which will create enormous problems in order to clear up a minor source of inequity. On the corporate tax side it is well known
1232

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
that if the tax rates on dividends and capital gains were at the same level, the tax provisions relating to these could be simplified enormously. With this is mind, the tax gap between dividends and capital gains has been narrowed by increasing the dividend tax credit. This is fine as far as it goes, but it stops short of situations where there is non-arm's length dealing.
For example, in these cases where corporate control is being transferred among family members, or an estate plan is being set up, very complex rules have been introduced to ensure that no untoward tax benefit accrues. Again we find the concern about equity and fairness. However, all this does is create a situation where grossly inordinate amounts of time and effort, not to mention money, are spent to cope with the tax ramifications of every private corporate change, and the revenue in question is minute.
In short, major simplification is being held up on the corporate side because of relatively minor equity problems. The cost of refusing to simplify the corporate tax provisions, not to mention partnership, trust resource or insurance provisions, is simply staggering. All of this is not to suggest that fairness and equity in our tax system should be abandoned or ignored. On the contrary, the reform of Canada's tax laws to make them more equitable is an important task. A sense of proportion is required, and a realization that the cost to achieve perfect equity may very well far exceed the minor benefit derived. In these troubled times, the removal of minor inequities should not be the primary end toward which the tax amendments should point. Rather, our major objective must be the stimulation of the economy. The introduction of effective incentives for the expansion of the economy has to take precedence over all else.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has, to some degree, recognized the need for incentives. Perhaps he has not recognized the need for effective incentives. Nowhere is this more clear than in the case of the $100 tax cut for low and middle income earners, of which we have heard so much in this House. The minister has told us that the cut will be concentrated in January and February, that a married taxpayer with two children could receive maximum benefits at income levels of up to about $16,000, and that a total of $700 million in revenue is expected to be returned.
This rebate appears generous in its gross amount. However, to the individual taxpayer it will represent very little. A taxpayer with three dependants is going to derive very little benefit from the cut which averages out to $1.92 per week for the year. It will also do little to offset the gap between the rate recommended by the Anti-Inflation Board for wage increases and the projected rate of inflation for this year. The tax cut is supposed to spur consumer spending and confidence in the economy, but its inevitable failure will serve only to undermine whatever confidence is left. Even the Economic Council of Canada, normally a rather mild mannered and optimistic body, concurs with this diagnosis.
The measures outlined in the minister's speech were described by the Economic Council as being so inadequate as to "barely prevent the currently high unemployment from increasing further". It went on to say that incentives proposed by the minister "will not be sufficient to bring about the reductions in either youth or adult unemployment that are needed".
The response of the Minister of Finance to this critical report which proposed a variety of alternative solutions to Canada's economic woes, was to label it irresponsible. Before accepting this assertion regarding the Economic Council's forecasts, it might be instructive to examine the government's record in this department.
In the budget of May, 1976, the then finance minister forecast a decline in unemployment. It rose, instead. The government anticipated a fiscal 1977 cash requirement, excluding foreign exchange, of $4.5 billion. In fact 1977 cash requirements were $5.4 billion, in excess of the forecast by 20 per cent.
According to that budget there would be a significant decline in the 1978 cash requirements from the level first forecast for 1977. Latest estimates reveal 1977 cash requirements nearly double those originally projected for 1977.
Only last March the government forecast 4 per cent real growth, 6 per cent inflation, and a $6.4 billion cash requirement. Where are they now? Today we are confronted with real growth of 2 per cent, inflation pushing 9 per cent, and an $8.5 billion cash requirement. The Minister of Finance should re-identify the target of his allegations of irresponsibility in forecasting.
The plain truth is that there is simply not enough incentive being introduced to stimulate the private sector. It is this sector upon which we must depend for the creation of the jobs our unemployed so urgently need.
Some obvious indicators of the plight in which the private sector finds itself lie in Canada's balance of international payments. The biggest single item in the balance is merchandise trade. Although we have recovered from a deficit in 1975 and appear to be on our way to a healthy surplus for 1977, a closer examination of the figures will show that all is not well.
Most of Canada's exports are natural resources shipped in raw or semi-processed form, while imports are generally made up of manufactured goods. In 1976, raw and semi-processed goods composed 66 per cent of exports, worth $25 billion, while manufactured products composed 61 per cent of imports for a value of $23 billion.
The problem lies in the fact that these raw exports have a very low labour input, whereas the manufactured imports have a high labour component. In other words, our exports create very few jobs in Canada relative to the number of foreign jobs created by our imports.
In the years from 1970 to 1976 our trade deficit in manufactured goods alone grew from $2.5 billion to over $10 billion,

November 24, 1977

and is currently projected to exceed $11 billion. Clearly the manufacturing sector is one to which the present bill might more effectively turn its attention.
Not only positive measures, in the form of incentives, are needed. The elimination of negative factors, whether in place or proposed in this bill, has to be examined. There is lack of co-ordination between the federal government and the governments of the provinces on matters concerning taxation.
A prime example of the disorganization that abounds is in the taxation of mining companies. In British Columbia and Saskatchewan, for example, the lack of co-operation and consultation between the two levels of government has led to a situation where the combination of provincial royalty payments, and the federal elimination of the income tax deduction for such payments, has effectively created a tax rate of more than 100 per cent of revenue. How can the government seriously talk about turning the economy around and attracting investment when it cannot even co-ordinate its taxes and those of the provinces to avoid placing companies in such an outrageous position? What confidence should a prospective investor have in such an administration? How the government can purport to be attracting investment on the one hand, while terrorizing business on the other, I do not know.
A further example of the double-edge sword of government programs can be seen in the Canadian home insulation program. Even ignoring the tremendous inroads that the federal conditions for the implementation of this program have made on the jurisdiction of the provinces, there are aspects which cry out for examination and change. The aspect that concerns us most with respect to this measure is that the grant will be added to the income of the spouse with the highest income. This makes a mockery of the entire program.
An insulation grant will only cover two thirds of the cost of materials involved, nothing is paid towards the actual installation. An applicant receiving the maximum grant of $350 would have to spend a minimum of $525 on materials. If added on to that were say $175 for installation, the minimum cost would be $750, against which the grant would be applied. But a homeowner with sufficient funds to be able to afford part of the cost of the insulating will find that the grant, when added to his taxable income, could easily be taxed at a rate of 40 per cent or more. He would then be left with a net grant of perhaps $200, which would cover barely one quarter of the total cost. In addition, the government has overlooked the fact that, in many cases, the insulating it has promoted will result in increased local taxes for the homeowner far in excess of his anticipated savings in energy costs. All this hardly represents an effective incentive program to encourage insulation.
The same label can be placed on this entire package of government proposals that we are discussing here today: ineffective. There are several reason why. First is the fact that not enough incentive is being given to stimulate the economy effectively. Those measures that are included are so weak as to be of doubtful use; our economy is not in so healthy a position that half hearted measures will improve it.
Income Tax
Connected with the lack of incentives is the continued and needless complexity of the income tax laws. Unconscionable amounts of time are spent by businessmen and their advisers trying to understand the provisions and then to apply them to their particular situations. This is bad enough for large companies which can afford to keep tax specialists on staff, but it is absolutely intolerable for small businessmen for whom this represents a major expense. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I wonder how many in this Chamber prepare their own income tax returns.
The government must make a commitment to streamline and simplify our tax laws and regulations. The major problem with this legislation, however, lies not so much in its content as in its style, for it is nothing more than another piece in the patchwork quilt that is the government's approach to the economy. We have here simply a few more palliative measures, designed to fix up the failures of the past, and destined to be replaced by the failures of the future.
The government is blindly slapping a few more band aids on the flagging economy in the hope that one of them might cover a wound. But the problem is far more complex than that, and so is the solution. Until the government realizes this, and takes a far-sighted and comprehensive approach to economic planning, we will continue to suffer the despair of unfulfilled potential that has been our lot for so many years.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join this debate on Bill C-ll but I will not get into the specifics of the bill. I intend to raise several very pointed questions when the bill goes to committee of the whole, at which time the minister, who is not present tonight, will be in his place. My remarks tonight are of a general nature and are more directed to what is not in the bill than to what is there.
Before I really begin I must say I am somewhat bothered that by reason of courtesy to my colleagues I am unable to take the full time which would normally be allotted to me, because the government has decided to bring in closure. That restricts the right of the opposition to scrutinize this legislation. This Bill has some critically important aspects to it, and the omissions in some cases are also very critical.
Yesterday the government charged that we were obstructing parliament and holding up the bill-the word "filibustering" was not used-when in fact up until the time of the closure motion only about 28 hours had been spent debating this legislation. If that amount of time was divided by the number of members in this House, a grand total of six minutes and 18 seconds would have been allowed for each hon. member to contribute to what is a critical tax proposal.
Shame!

The minister does not want to call it a budget, but if it is not a budget, it should be. The hon. member

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has been calling on the government to bring in a budget before Christmas.
1 reject the notion of the government that restricting my right to speak on this legislation is proper. I feel almost professorial at this point because I want to lecture-if I can use that word-the government about the nature of parliamentary democracy. I do not deny for a moment the right of the government, which has a clear majority, to set fiscal and monetary policies. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has just walked in, and I will say very clearly to him that it is his prerogative, responsibility, and indeed his duty to set fiscal and monetary policies and to bring in a budget. It is his duty to set the rate of taxation and to get the economy in order.
It is the prerogative of the government to set foreign policy. It is the right of the government, which has a majority, in a parliamentary system to rule and govern absolutely. I do not debate that point, but what I do reject is any move by any government to deny my rights, privileges, responsibilities, and duties to all the citizens of Canada and in particular, of course, to the people of Selkirk. It is my responsibility to scrutinize, to oppose, and to offer alternatives, and the alternatives we have offered this government are endless.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe and my leader have been very specific point by point, particularly in the area of fiscal and monetary policies and in suggesting a new budget. If it is true-and I believe it is-that the government has the absolute right to govern, surely the opposition has the absolute right to oppose, to scrutinize, and to take our time, if that is what we deem responsible, to try to persuade the government with reasonable arguments based on sound judgment, however reluctant it is to do anything meaningful, that it ought to take a course of action which will mean something to the country. I do not take it at all lightly that I am forced to curtail my remarks because the government has brought in closure.

speechtext: Give us five minutes of something original.

The hon. member wants something original. I can tell him there is nothing original on his side of the House because we are getting more of what we have had in past years, deficits. I must correct myself because there is some-

thing new this year. The deficit is larger than it was last year. We are facing a $9 billion deficit. Perhaps some of my hon. colleagues opposite do not really understand what $9 billion can buy. So that they might understand-because they spend money as if it were water, and they obviously do not understand the consequences of a $9 billion deficit-I will tell them how much $9 billion is.
Let us take a 1978 Dodge Aspen sports sedan with a standard shift, and no options. That car sells for about $4,700. It is about 197 inches long, which is about 16.3 feet. Let us line Dodge Aspens up bumper to bumper along the Trans-Canada Highway beginning at Victoria. The line would stretch all the way across British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, that great keystone province of Manitoba which has a Tory government, all across Ontario, winding its way down around the Great Lakes, all through that great la belle province, which will remain in Confederation because a Canada without Quebec is no Canada at all, down through the maritimes to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia-we could not get to Prince Edward Island on the Trans-Canada which, incidentally, is something else the government has balked on-then over to the capital of Newfoundland, St. John's, to a location in front of Joey's oratory. The total distance I have here is 4,860 miles. That is as of September 3, 1962. If we lined all those cars up bumper to bumper, an amount equal to our deficit would pay for every single car, and there would be $1.5828408 billion and a few pennies left over. That is what our deficit means, and yet this budget is the same as usual. That is obviously of no concern to the government.
Hon. members opposite smile with contentment about this mini-budget, economic statement, or whatever the minister chooses to call it. A million Canadians are unemployed, and hon. members opposite dare to ask me to be original. With unanimous consent I would yield the floor so that the hon. member for York-Simcoe, for the benefit of hon. members opposite who may not have heard him the first time, might again shed some light on what ought to be done and must be done to get the country working again.
This bill, this budget or this economic statement-whatever it is-says nothing about housing. My colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), smiles, but I know it is a smile of great disappointment because this matter almost passes the point of seriousness. There is not a word in this bill about housing. There is not a penny for housing. I think it is important that I read what the deputy minister under the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has said about housing, while this bill or whatever it is is absolutely silent with reference to housing. In a speech made in Calgary in September, 1976, Mr. Teron said:
When 280,000 families in Canada pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing and 500,000 families in Canada pay more than 35 per cent, and 820,000 families pay more than 25 per cent, and when 2/3 of those Canadians in need of housing cannot afford to buy or rent a home without a government subsidy, we have a problem of fundamental proportions. We must take decisive action now or face unparalleled problems later.
November 24, 1977

One year and two months later there is no sign that the government has heeded the deputy minister of urban affairs.
I hope the Minister of Finance and hon. members opposite will not consider my remarks to be partisan or critical, which is the normal role of a member of the opposition, when as a member concerned about housing I plead with them to consider some of the concrete and constructive proposals put forward by the leader of my party, by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, and by other members of this party. We are not looking for glory or praise for the Conservative party, but are here because of an interest and a love for this country. Our suggestions are put forward in a spirit of co-operation.
There is nothing in this mini-budget to solve the critical problems Mr. Teron has referred to, nor is there anything to answer the problem of energy conservation as it applies to urban transportation. I have said in this Chamber before, and I think it is worth saying again, that at the moment three quarters of our population live in urban centres, and in another ten or 12 years 90 per cent will live in cities. Half of the energy consumed in this country is spent on intracity transportation. The larger cities like Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal have modern energy saving mass transit systems that are efficient and energy saving. The Minister of Finance and this government, however, have reneged on a 1974 election promise of hundreds of millions of dollars for mass transportation within our urban centres.
To state the obvious, we must begin to do things, and right now. Of course hon. members opposite will ask the usual question-where are we going to get the money? They blame the Tories for asking them to spend money all the time, and claim we have more programs than can possibly be financed.
We reiterate almost to exhaustion the solution we have proposed. It is not what you spend, it is how you spend. Time and time again we have asked the government to get its priorities in order. We only have to go up to the sixth floor of this building and gaze across that great river to the great province of Quebec, the great city of Hull. Spread almost as far as the eye can see are those fortresses that house civil servants.
Let it not be said that we on this side criticize civil servants. We could point to almost any civil servant and say he works hard and conscientiously. The question is not whether he works hard, it is whether the work is necessary. As the Auditor General pointed out, the government cannot control its spending. We have asked over and over again that it set priorities, and certainly the most obvious areas of capital expenditure are office buildings and accommodation.
If time permitted, Mr. Speaker, I could give a list as long as an arm and a leg of ways the government could save money so that problems of energy conservation and urban transportation could be solved. Not only that, we could export the technology and finance our own urban transit systems through selling our knowledge abroad. We have the brain power and the technology; the only thing lacking is the initiative on the part of the government. I do not believe the government has that much vision, however. I believe its members are stale, worn out,
