tired. They offer the -same old non-solutions to problems like one million people unemployed and deficits going up to $9 billion. The Canadian dollar was worth 90 cents yesterday, and for all I know it may only be worth 88 cents today.
We on this side plead with the government, even at this 11th hour, to show some sign of repentance by bringing in a budget. We would be overjoyed if that were done before Christmas and would co-operate so that this House might address the problems besetting the country.
At committee stage, Mr. Speaker, I shall be asking specific questions on specific parts of this bill. This party will do all it can in a responsible way to make Bill C-ll address, to some small degree, the problems of Canada. For the sake of the country we in the opposition can do no less.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate on Bill C-ll I should like to be rather positive tonight. This government needs some sincere suggestions from all sides to ensure that in the short time left at its disposal as a government it can start solving some of the problems facing us.
We need your help.

As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) says, he needs our help, and I can assure him that he will have it tonight.
Many of my colleagues have pointed out deficiencies or aspects of Bill C-ll that should be clarified. Many of those points will be dealt with in committee of the whole when it starts later tonight or tomorrow. Mr. Speaker, I think in the dialogue that will then ensue on such things as the proposal to tax the insulation and a grant that was given by this government, as well as such things as the proposal to tax the insurance cash surrender values to some extent, which is proposed in this bill, the whole reference that is made in the bill to the turnover, roll-over provisions with regard to small businesses and farms are now in the hands of say, a father who wishes to turn the property over to his children, all of these matters raised by my colleagues hopefully will be dealt with fully during the committee of the whole session. There are other items, the $100 tax credit which many have referred to. We feel that while the concept was, I suppose, stolen from us, it is a good concept. There are certain clarifications that are very badly needed.
One thing I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, and I hope this time when we get to the committee of the whole, the Minister of Finance will be able to give us some insight of this, I feel there are a lot of questions to be asked, and hopefully answered, with respect to the $9 billion borrowing limit extension which the minister has included in this bill. $9 billion is a lot of money. It is a lot of money when you consider that it is almost as much as the total federal spending budget at the time when this Trudeau government took power ten years ago.

November 24, 1977
Income Tax
I said this evening I would like to be positive, and I mean that. What I hope to do tonight, in addition to dealing with Bill C-ll, is to make certain suggestions to the House, to the government and to the Minister of Finance as to how we could handle more effectively this whole budgetary process, which this House has to grapple with periodically, and specifically this legislation before us tonight. In doing that, I think it will be helpful if we basically accept, that in any budget, there are two sides to it. There is a policy side, which is by far the most important, and there is also what might be regarded as an administrative or a structural side. It is this technical side we are dealing with tonight. Generally, because budgets have those two aspects to them, and realizing of necessity, they are relatively complicated documents, I feel there should be certain tactics or approaches taken in order to facilitate, not only our dialogue and discussion of the matter before us, but hopefully to facilitate better understanding by the Canadian public as to what this process is all about.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with four or five suggestions with respect to that question of structural change. How can we get a more effective approach in dealing with a bill touching on income tax, for instance, Bill C-ll?
My suggestion would be that green papers should be used more widely by the government because I believe green papers are well received. For example, we had green papers on sales tax, on the charity areas, and they contributed to a meaningful debate and discussion with respect to the points raised in those green papers. I would hope, therefore, that the government would bring in more green papers with respect to matters they feel are suitable to that kind of discussion. The next point I would like to raise tonight is that I believe the time has come for less secrecy surrounding this whole question of budgetmaking and the type of debate taking place here. Let me just give you one example. It is widely known, although somehow it is kept secret, that the Department of Finance calls on various consulting firms for advice. For reasons not clear to me, the names of those consultants are not disclosed, we are not advised as to their terms of reference, and I think we should be. I cannot see anything wrong with the Department of Finance making it very clear that they have called on a certain accountant firm, a certain law firm, or have called on certain tax professionals for advice as to what they should do. I suggest we should have a little less secrecy. Let us open up and let us know who the government is relying on for that type of consultative information or advice.
When the minister says tonight he needs our help, I think he needs the help of others, and I would like to see the Minister of Finance surround himself with an advisory group of people well vested in tax matters so that the minister can get some fresh advice. I say that because there is a growing suspicion that the advice the minister is getting is warmed over, old advice, which is something the officials around him are attracted to, but you don't have that spark of ingenuity or freshness that might be conveyed in the policy thinking sessions a new independent advisory group drawn preferably from

the private sector might bring into the general policy-making decision apparatus.
I would like to see draft legislation made available to the House, not only for our consideration but so that the general public can have a look at what the public has in mind. Sometimes I feel that we tend to get locked in here, the government will introduce a bill, it will go through first reading-which is only a formality-it comes to second reading and they suddenly feel they are locked into a position that if they alter or back away from, this is a loss of face. It then results in that impossible situation where we make a comment, or the public makes a comment with respect to changes and the government feels they cannot even meet those changes without appearing to be backing down from a position they got themselves into by introducing the bill in the first place. Why is it we cannot have draft legislation on the routine type of legislation, which is what Bill C-ll is mainly made up of? Let us take a look at it. Let us find out, without people taking definitive positions, what the general public might feel about draft legislation, and also have a free interchange within the House, both opposition and government members concerning their views on a draft put before us.
Tomorrow when we get to committee of the whole stage with Bill C-ll, I think we will be uncomfortably surprised as to how little will be told as to why changes now proposed in Bill C-ll are needed. Why should that be so? For every change that is proposed in any bill, not only fiscal bills such as we have before us, why can't we have every change in legislation be given an in depth honest answer as to why the change is needed?
On a money matter, for instance, the first clause in Bill C-ll deals with capital gains. I think we should have an explanation from the minister on that. Why does he feel the $1,000 write-off or chargeable amount with regard to capital gains losses should be raised to $2,000? I think we should rightly expect the minister to tell us what revenues are involved, how many transactions are involved, why are all losses with respect to capital gains not in a position that they can be written off against capital gains. That type of thing I believe will be very meaningful, and I hope when I mention this item tonight, the minister will cooperate during the committee of the whole stage to give the answers which have rarely been given before as to why the changes are really needed. Let me touch on a bigger question, the concern of any minister of finance, the policy side of the budget.
We have touched on the structural aspect. Let us turn to the policy side of the budget. In this connection I think it would be extremely helpful if there were more references to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs concerning the economic condition of the country. This has often been discussed. Other Ministers of Finance have hinted that they might make such general references, but for reasons known only to themselves they draw back at the last moment when it comes to giving the committee a firm reference to

enable it to consider, for example, what are the real alternatives for Canada today faced with inflation, lack of real growth, and mounting trade deficits. What, for instance, in such circumstances are the effects of tax cuts or reductions in sales taxes? Let us have more references to our standing committee so that we can consider policy matters under the heading of the economic climate in Canada.
I have touched on the policy questions which arise from every budget. Here is an example of the need for separation. Let there be two distinct parts of every budget with a clear distinction between the policy side and what one might refer to as the structural side.
Most of us eventually feel sorry for the poor Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay) over there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He is a happy fellow.

I should like to make him a little happier, then, by giving him a bit more to do. I am suggesting that more bills of a structural nature be introduced by the Minister of National Revenue. Why, for example, should he not bring in the various bills whose administration he has to supervise? This is a suggestion which might be considered in future as a step ahead in trying to get through the rather extensive procedure we now follow as far as budgets are concerned.
Another suggestion. It may be that to iron out hundreds, if not thousands of misunderstandings which arise with respect to the tax process and the position of the government with regard to income tax, some type of board ought to be established which could deal with this task in a prompt and effective way. I do not mean a board in the sense of an adjudication board, but a board which could address itself to difficulties and inequities which are inherent in our taxation system, and advise whether they should be altered in the next budget. This would, if you like, constitute a screening process to ensure a more effective, a more efficiency-oriented income tax approach.
These are only a few suggestions having to do with the process in which we are engaged tonight. I should like to turn now in a more general way to the whole question of the economic position in which the country finds itself. I should like to touch upon the incomparable incompetence of the government in dealing with economic matters. Many times I have heard the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Finance speaking about restraint and suggesting that somehow or other they know how to cut down federal spending. Mr. Speaker, I feel this is just like asking a rabbit to carry lettuce. Neither of those two gentlemen knows how to restrain public expenditure.
Tell us what to cut.

The President of the Treasury Board says. "Tell us what to cut." I hope he will remain in his place, because he will get an earful as I speak. In the past decade Canada's economic performance has deteriorated, with Ottawa giving little priority to measures which might arrest
Income Tax
the trend. On balance, the measures taken by the government have aggravated rather than relieved the situation. Meanwhile, grizzly economic figures pile up.
Unemployment, running at more than 8 per cent-twice the level forecast by the Economic Council for this period-will likely result in more than one million jobless this winter. Inflation roars on at nearly 9 per cent, well above the government's target and three times the level anticipated by the Economic Council. Trade in the last quarter fell to a projected annual deficit of $6.5 billion, the highest in history, at a time when the administration actually anticipated a decrease. The government's budgetary deficits average over $5 billion a year. Next year it will be something like $11 billion. In the aggregate, government deficits in the past ten years have totalled more than the combined deficits of all federal governments in the previous 100 years.
The Canadian travel deficit reached over $400 million in the last quarter, a tenfold increase compared to four years ago, and it is anticipated this deficit will approach $2 billion for the year. Our dollar in relation to the United States dollar has slipped 13 cents since last November to its present 90 cents. Our foreign exchange reserves have slumped to their lowest level since 1971, and now represent only l'/2 months of our imports. In this connection it is most disappointing to find in the Conference Board Report issued today that the effect of our 13-cent devaluation has simply been to restore the cost of inflation since 1975. I should like to quote exactly what the Conference Board said on this point:
The effect of the recent devaluation has been, therefore, to offset the increase in relative labour earnings which has occurred since 1975.
In short, here we have a government which, through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), and to a lesser extent through certain other ministers, has tried to tell the Canadian people that the 90-cent dollar is something good. Well, the Conference Board tells us that the effect of devaluation has simply been to offset the rise in wages which has occurred on account of inflation in this country since the control program began.
Productivity among our workers continues to lag compared to productivity in other countries, making us relatively noncompetitive internationally. Here again I should like to refer hon. members to the Conference Board study which came out today. It shows that in 83 industries reviewed by the Board, wages in Canada have been higher than comparable wages in the United States, yet productivity on the average has been only about 90 per cent of that of their United States counterparts. Investor confidence is at a low with stock exchange values crumbling year by year in real terms.
This economic morass is illustrated by our low real growth, that is, growth without inflation. For the past three years how many of us realize-certainly I do not believe the government realizes-that such annual real growth has been stalled on a per capita basis at one half of one per cent. In the past reported year the United States real growth on the other hand

Income Tax
has been 4.6 per cent, nine times the actual real growth in the same one-year period in Canada.
I said at the beginning I intended to be positive, and I will be positive tonight. Those are the bald facts. That is the situation into which this government has put us. Now I would like to make some suggestions of a policy nature that I hope the government will accept in order to get us out of the problems we face. In making these points, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to divide them into short term policies, middle term policies, and longer term policies. But first I would suggest that to restore public confidence in our economic momentum in Canada we need leadership in Ottawa which is willing to implement the three types of plans that I have indicated; that is, short term, middle term, and longer term plans. In short, an industrial strategy for the nation must be evolved.
With respect to short term policies we have said for some time that, faced with today's unemployment and sluggish economic growth, there should be substantial personal income tax cuts, with the greatest benefit being given to those earning less than $8,000 per year and with lesser benefits being extended to those earning between $8,000 and $16,000. The lower the income, the greater should be the benefit. The government in Bill C-ll has met the suggestion at least in part, but unfortunately it proposes that the $100 tax credit will be felt in 1978, not now.
Ministers have represented that the tax credit will be shared by Canadians in January or February, but there is no place in this bill that that is said to be the case. They plan to do that through new directives in an administrative way. I emphasize it is going to be an administrative matter, and we will be suggesting why it should not be left in that position. The burden of financing public expenditures has fallen increasingly on personal income taxpayers. This tax has essentially affected low and middle income taxpayers who receive the bulk of income in Canada.
How many of us realize that in 1975, the latest year for which data is available, over 60 per cent of the total income taxes paid in this country was paid by persons earning under $20,000 per year? I have said repeatedly, certainly for the last 18 months, the federal government should reduce the load that it is taking from the personal income taxpayers. Again, we believe the federal government should reduce its manufacturer sales tax as soon as possible. This would bring about a reduction in the consumer price index and would boost consumer and business confidence. It would also increase consumer purchasing power.
Although unemployment is national in scope, its greatest burden is borne by the five eastern provinces, and by young people entering the labour force. Companies willing to create employment in those regions, or for young people, must be given suitable added incentives. For example, tax credits or rebates could be made available to corporations willing to create jobs in regions with high unemployment. This would encourage, I would suggest, those companies to invest needed capital. But that is only half of the job.
In addition there should be unemployment tax credits for firms which qualify for such assistance by hiring additional workers. Such employment assistance ought to be oriented most heavily to our youth and to those securing jobs in high unemployment areas. The minister in his October 20 statement made reference to employment tax credits. He indicated that they would like to put a program in position, but I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, there has been no action. There is no legislation. Frankly, the government is not sure how it will implement that program. Mr. Speaker, we would like to tell it how to implement the program. I can assure you if we were the government in this House tonight, such a program would be on the statute books of Canada.
Tell us what you would do.

Mr. Speaker, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has asked that I give him some hints. I can assure him that if he can succeed in getting the Minister of Finance at least to attend the meetings of that committee we will start giving him some hints. So the ball is over to you, Mr. Speaker.
Wage and price controls, in our view, have a limited usefulness. Left in place, they become counter productive and a deterrent to economic expansion. Therefore the government should commence phasing out its present wage and price control program right now. An ongoing monitoring agency may be needed for a limited time, but it is the market place that should be left as much as possible to settle wage and price levels. Given fiscal and monetary restraint by government, the market place in the past has controlled inflation, and it can do so in the future.
Surely it is relevant to note that in the past three months the inflation level in the United States has been an average 3.8 per cent a year. Compare that to the level in Canada, over 8 per cent-twice the level that has been experienced in the last three months in the United States. That is not just a three month phenomenon. The fact is that since controls were put in place in Canada we have consistently had higher inflation levels than they have had in the United States where they have no controls. That is something the government loves to gloss over in its fascination with the controls program in Canada that has contributed to tens of thousands of Canadians being out of work on account of the counter productive nature of controls in undermining business confidence in the country. But, Mr. Speaker, I have touched on just a few of what I regard as short term policies.
Perhaps the more important policies are the medium term, longer term policies in which this government is so lacking. Let me touch on some medium term policies I would like them to consider. Governments, in particular the federal government, have increased their share of the economy in the past decade so that they now handle about 43 per cent of our total gross national product. This, I would suggest, has placed an unfair burden on our personal income taxpayers and has contributed to inflation, lower productivity, and in fact has ruined many small businessmen. For these reasons we believe it is impera-

November 24, 1977

tive that government should reduce its gross national product take to a more manageable level.
In conjunction with other levels of government, a five-year target for reduced government spending in relation to our gross national product must be set and reached. The government likes to assure us that it is trying to control its spending so that it will not rise more quickly than the GNP. In short, it is saying that it will maintain its share of government spending at its present relative relationship to the GNP. Frankly, that is not good enough. What is the magic in all governments taking 43 per cent of the GNP? Clearly it has contributed to some of our problems. Governments must start retrenching to return to a lower share of the gross national product.
Zero budgeting is a concept which must be introduced to public administration. It would ensure that programs would have to be periodically reviewed and justified. The present assumption that once a program begins it continues indefinitely, which all socialists seem to assume, must be changed.
In addition, working with labour, business and consumer groups, the government should establish targets for future real growth, inflation, and employment levels within the country. With such guidelines, decision makers within the economy will be able to proceed with greater confidence in the future. As targets are reached, confidence will grow. If targets are not reached, reappraisals to determine the reasons will be beneficial.
We have not heard from the Minister of Finance in this respect. I think his predecessor shocked most members of this House, when asked why would he not set such targets for Canada, he said that it was because they might cause a lack of confidence in the government. That is one of the reasons for governments establishing targets. One wants to have a bench mark to judge them by in order to see if a reasonable target has been met; if not, why not; and if the government cannot do it, we will get another one.
Canada is the most over governed country in the world. Not only do we have four levels of government in most areas, but we find these levels duplicate activities and on occasion stalemate, or at least frustrate each other's actions. At the federal level we must question if it is necessary to have 25 different departments which are duplicated in the main at the provincial level. Is it really necessary to have a federal Department of the Environment concerned about pollution, or could it not be assumed that if each provincial environmental department enforced anti-pollution legislation there would be no dirty federal air in Canada?
Is it necessary for federal authorities to add to our already high housing prices through their needless regulations and requirements? There may be a role for the federal authority to play as banker in connection with housing, but the actual development and construction of such housing should be a provincial matter.
Traditionally, small businessmen have been Canada's main employers, yet today they are under heavier pressure than any
Income Tax
other business group. Tax concessions help, but other steps are needed. Many smaller businessmen never reach a taxable earnings level before they are snuffed out. It is here that aid is needed. Less regulation by government would be a tonic for such entrepreneurs. Dealing with regulations is an added cost for big business, and it kills the small fellow.
At this point I should like to remind the Minister of Finance that at page 8 of "The Way Ahead" the government outlined eight crucial steps it was going to take during the anti-inflation program, which it indicated would help relieve the various problems I am touching upon tonight. Not one of the eight has been executed to date. I hope the Minister of Finance will be able to tell us why the government failed with respect to what it set out to do.
Consideration should be given to assisting smaller firms in the formation of consortia which would enable them to compete better with larger firms. Grouping smaller concerns by specialty would preserve the individual identity of each, while allowing the consortia to bid for large orders both domestically and internationally. An increase in subcontracting by large concerns to smaller businessmen would revitalize our economy. Government, which is the largest purchaser of goods, must ensure that small businessmen get a fair share of the orders.
Federal and provincial minimum wage laws have contributed to our lack of competitiveness in that Canadian minimum wages are now 20 per cent to 30 per cent higher than in the United States. Not only have they contributed on our cost side, but also they have contributed to our unemployment where many people who might hire, if it were not for the minimum wage structure, now simply do not hire. Is it better to have a person out of work on unemployment insurance, or at least working for a wage, as opposed to the present situation?
The federal minimum wage of $2.85 an hour compares to the United States minimum wage of $2.30. The American Congress recently boosted their minimum wage to $2.65 an hour effective next January, to $2.85 a year later, and to $3.05 in 1980. It would be wise for federal and provincial authorities to freeze any further increases in our minimum wages until the Americans at least catch up. In certain fields such as the tourist industry it may be necessary to make further minimum wage exemptions in order for them to regain some competitiveness. As minimum wage laws are a major cause of youth unemployment we should consider a short run subsidy, such as a six months' subsidy to youths just entering the private sector labour market who otherwise would be unemployed, if full minimum wages had to be paid.
One must consider the leverage one receives if a person's wage is subsidized. At $3 per hour, if the government were to subsidize that wage for $1 up to six months, and assuming the person works 40 hours a week-that is $120-of that amount approximately $30 comes back in taxes, and the net subsidy paid out of the federal treasury would be $10 per worker. On the other hand if he is put on unemployment insurance and if he receives $120 comparable to the $120 wage I am referring to, the government gets approximately $30 in income taxes. Thus, the total net cost to the federal treasury is $90. In short,

Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for their courtesy in allowing me to continue my remarks, but as I was saying I feel that I would like to make some long term policy suggestions to the government.
World technology is changing at a rapid rate. Canada has failed to keep abreast of these changes, and this has contributed to our $10 billion manufacturing trade deficit, a deficit that might grow to $ 11.5 billion this year.
The deterioration in our net export position in 1976-the deficit on trade in goods and services accounted for 2.7 per cent of the gross national product-is perhaps the most important shift that has taken place in the Canadian economy. We are simply consuming more than we are producing. We are living beyond our means and using borrowed foreign money to cover the difference.
While other nations have concentrated on encouraging and funding new technology breakthroughs, we have tended to fund existing industries which have grown uncompetitive. American government funding of research and development is twice as high as ours in relation to the respective GNPs.
The Japanese strategy is to increase the international sales effort for existing products and to develop new products through government sponsored research. The Japanese government spent $214 million over the past five years to help the computer industry compete with IBM's series 370. Canada has no similar programs, but on the other hand will spend this year two and a half times that amount on the CBC.
We no longer have a full time minister of science and technology in Canada. We should.
We believe there must be a massive effort to assist Canadian business to attain technology breakthroughs in fields in which we have an inherent advantage. These fields include agriculture, the resources of our three seas, our fresh water, and those industries related to our mineral and chemical wealth.
Historically we have been large exporters of pulp and paper products. Plantations in South America and Europe are now producing marketable trees in six to ten years, compared to our 40 or 50 years. Faced with this problem federal complacency is unforgiveable. The government's $100 million financing of overseas pulp and paper plants, which will compete with us, for example in Poland, is madness.
A more imaginative internatioenal sales effort at the federal level is overdue. Properly merchandized, Canadian produce could be sold more effectively. Cheese factories are closing down in this country, but at the same time Canadian Cheddar cheese is being rationed in England because it is in short supply. Can you believe it, Mr. Speaker?
Our export financing, which is in the billions, has become the private preserve of a few intimates of the Liberal party. It must be made available to all exporters, both small and large.
We have lost the balance in Canada between big corporations and those not so big. It must be regained so that the traditional ingenuity, inventiveness, and entrepreneurship of
November 24, 1977

small businessmen can once again contribute to the growth of our productivity.
As the world is reshaped into new market pools we must also seek out partners to enlarge our trade areas. With our natural resources and our proximity to the wealthiest market in the world, we are in an excellent position to gain access to such markets. In the meantime the government must stop allowing important industries to be ravaged by foreign competition. There is no reason why Canada should become the freest of the free trade nations in the world. Through it all we need an industrial strategy to chart once again the course which will restore our economy to its real growth potential with full employment and stable prices.
When we have an opportunity to vote on Bill C-11, we will do so feeling that many of the measures in the bill are good. We are not against the $100 tax credit, but essentially we believe that the government must improve Bill C-ll. We hope that it will improve it during committee of the whole stage and that we will be able to vote with it on third reading. Frankly, as it now stands, we cannot see how we can vote with the government at third reading if Bill C-l 1 remains in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I would not have spoken tonight if, while walking between the parliament buildings, I had not asked myself in terms of taxation, what is all this for? As I hear the government members speak about restraint and as I watch the government shove the crumbs off the table while crying for restraint, thus demonstrating its tremendous hypocrisy, I feel the need to rise tonight to speak on this Bill C-ll amending the Income Tax Act. 1 ask: taxation for what? Is it taxation to light another massive structure on the other side of the river? There are half empty offices in Ottawa and half empty offices in Hull.
Oh, oh!

I see that makes hon. members opposite a little concerned. They should be concerned, because if all Canadians could travel to Ottawa today and see the half empty offices in Hull and in Ottawa they too would be concerned and would not believe a word of the government's restraint program. They too would see that this taxation bill, these crumbs they are sweeping to the Canadian people in an attempt to buy them with their own money, is of little interest. It is indeed discouraging. Do we need this further taxation to turn the lights on in these buildings?
One government member talks about conservation, about cutting back on the lighting in these buildings, yet when you look across the river you see the lights in all the government buildings in Hull blazing away. Is that what we need taxation for? I think not. Perhaps we need more taxation for foreign affairs because, after all, the government has not been able to give away all the money it budgeted for foreign affairs. There is no increase in taxes, the hon. member says? I say there is a constant increase in taxes. You have an increase in taxes through inflation.

Better get your facts straight.

Perhaps you do not need more taxes because you cannot spend all the money you have. You cannot give away the money fast enough. Right now in the Department of External Affairs officials in CIDA are furiously scrambling to try to spend the money quickly, because if they do not spend their full budget they know that next year they will be cut back. CIDA is spending $1 billion.
Go on to your next point.

Yet the report comes in that we have budgeted that $1 billion and we can only spend $913 million. The government has given money for every single project. There is not a country in the whole world that has come to us and told us they need foreign aid and was turned away. The government met all the demands, and still has money left over.
The government is giving away capital at a time when Canada needs capital for its development. What will it do with the surpluses in the external aid program? What will it do with that extra money that comes back to revenue? Perhaps it will give it back in some form of tax rebate-I hope so. It is the great give-away program. If it is not going to be given away by CIDA, perhaps it will be given away by establishing another embassy in another underdeveloped nation, and we will be more successful in giving money away next year. However, then again we will probably exercise restraint in the Middle East. We will not establish a new embassy or an expanded embassy in the Middle East where, in Saudi Arabia, they have $23 billion for which they are trying to find a place in the world. That $23 billion could be tapped through technology exchange if the government would care enough just to go to that country and establish and expand relations there. In Iraq there is $7 billion. We could establish a minor embassy, but there is no thrust into real world markets where there is in fact potential for dollars and for Canadian industry and trade.
If we could get into these great markets of the Middle East, we would not require such a large taxation bill. We could perhaps be giving back more money than this token $100 tax deduction which is promised to us. Perhaps we could have more money to put out another green paper.
The government is very effective at putting out green papers. Green papers are another stall tactic while the athletes of Canada starve or live on welfare or unemployment insurance. The athletes of Canada who contributed to Canada in the Olympics live below subsistence, and the government puts out another green paper. To the government the green paper is the answer to everything.
Perhaps some of the tax dollars the government did not give back but could have, and should have, should have gone to a place like Wickaninnish, but the government wants to close down Wickaninnish. That is a revenue producing vehicle. There are only 22 rooms involved, but the government wants

to cut this out and instead build some form of interpretative centre which will require more and more civil servants.
The government should cut back the number of civil servants. There would be a tremendous saving. There are 467,268 federal employees. That is far too many. Someone once mentioned to Milton Friedman that many government employees do not work hard at their jobs. He responded by saying, "That's good, they do less harm that way." There has been fantastic growth in the public service which is well reported and documented, and there is no doubt that Canadians are getting fed up with it.
This taxation policy is nothing new. It is a rehash. Why does the government not look at some new ideas? Why not a flat rate tax system where everyone would pay equally?
Come on!
Would that help the poor?
Is that Tory policy?

There are many basic economic policies which could be developed. Instead of getting more and more involved in the economy the government should adopt a policy which involves it less and less and which would move more and more toward a free economy. The government should interfere only in extreme cases, in order to maintain free enterprise. The government professes to believe in free enterprise, but 43 per cent of the gross national product goes in taxation. The government says it stands for competition, but its competition bill cannot get through the House and cannot establish any credibility in the country.
The government discourages price fixing while at the same time working on the international scene as a major price fixer itself.
A major reduction of taxation would come about with a reduction in the number of government employees. If the number of government employees were reduced, government spending would be reduced.
Keep that up and the voters will reduce you.

In the past the automatic answer was "get rid of useless jobs, abolish them," but today the unemployed and their families have become a tax burden. It becomes more and more impossible to keep them from being charges on the government and to develop more productive capacity in the private sector. One suggestion would be to acknowledge openly the existence of this powerful political force and present a compromise solution, from which all parties would benefit. The aim should be to encourage the thousands now on government payrolls to transfer voluntarily to private industry by making it financially attractive for them to do so. To that end all government employees working on jobs which are found to be unneeded and so designated as permanently abolished should be placed on a leave of absence with a full pay guarantee until the normal time of retirement.
[Mr. Wenman.1
Even if unneeded employees stayed home, the government would net tremendous savings in the cost of working space, supplies, and other expenses. The proposed program also calls for 10 per cent awards of whatever the employees who go into private industry earn there. Thus if an employee making $10,000 at a government job goes into private industry and earns $10,000, the total income would be $11,000, and the government would save $9,000.
The government should develop new economic programs, with new imagination and new policy thrust. Instead of the constant attitude that the government can spend itself out of its problems by hiring more civil servants to create more spending programs, the government should concentrate on developing productive programs in the private sector.
Undoubtedly when the report of the Auditor General comes forward it will discuss the expenditure of $59 million by the Canada Council. Undoubtedly it will express some concern that there is no accountability by this government for the $59 million so spent. That $59 million was handed to the Canada Council, and no accountability is required. The Canada Council took the money and allocated it to many individual applicants. These people make applications, receive money, and no further accountability is required. It is time that all Canada Council money was treated like other government funds and a measure of accountability established. When a Canada Council grant or contribution is provided, a legal contract should be established, the budget submitted met, and the project as submitted finished, or the person receiving the money should be held liable for it and the money should be returned.
The list of Canada Council grants would cause concern for any Canadian, and it does. I wonder how many Canadians would accept spending $20,000 for a film record of Pashtoon pastoralists in Afghanistan. I wonder how many Canadians would like to see their hard earned tax dollars going into that kind of project. Looking over this list I wonder how Canada will benefit by an annotated edition of the complete letters of Benjamin Disraeli for $113,000. I wonder how many Canadians will benefit from a critical edition of the correspondance of Emile Zola for $30,000. I wonder how many backbench Liberals would stand up and defend these Canada Council grants. Who will accept the responsibility for levying taxes for this type of project?
There are many items which could be discussed with regard to waste in government. These are becoming well known to a very disillusioned Canadian public. Of every dollar we earn 43 cents is now being consumed by taxation. I wonder how the constituents of hon. members opposite feel when the average Canadian who goes to work at nine o'clock in the morning has to work until 1.30 in the afternoon just to pay his taxes. Only after that does he begin earning his take-home pay.
I wonder how many people realize that of the $15,000 average salary, $7,000 goes to taxes in one form or another. I wonder how many Canadians realize that the equalization these tax acts claim to represent means no equalization at all
November 24, 1977

but rather an excessive burden on the taxpayers of Ontario, Alberta, and British Columbia. This taxation is not just reflected in grants and formats but is an equalization found throughout the structure of government from bill to bill.
In small craft harbours, boat owners in Vancouver pay $2 per foot for a berth whilst the cost in Quebec and the Maritimes is $1. That is hardly fair. Is it fair that a tax system sets up an equalization format which has western Canadians subsidizing the gasoline that eastern Canadians use in their cars whilst those cars cost westerners $500 or $600 more because of the freight rates?
This bill does not address any of the inequities in our taxation system. It is band aid legislation. Accountants and lawyers will have a heyday with it, yet they have hardly had time to adjust to the last tax bill. It is time the government brought in measures to deal effectively with the taxes it has already collected instead of throwing them away on CIDA programs, Canada Works programs, or Canada Council grants. The people of Canada are getting tired of this lack of accountability.
